pieces.html:
Nothing’s better than takin’ a good leak. Not even sex. I remember Uncle Rex telling me this when I was a kid, and I’ll be damned if it ain’t true. I dripped out and zipped up while she, my lady, emptied a can of beans into the cookpot.

“Dinner’s nearly ready, Earlie!”

Her voice was as sweet as iced tea in the Mississippi heat and thick enough to coat the inside of the cup. She brought the empty can out to the trash pile and gave me a disapproving look. She hated when I filled the cans that sat close to the house.

“Clean it up this time, Earl,” she said, eyeing the still-warm foam. “And don’t forget to wash your hands.”

After the fire, we lost a lot of things, habits o’ hygiene being one of ’em.

“Course, baby,” I cooed, wiping off on my long johns. “And what we got for dinner? Smells real good.”

“Oh, baby.” She smiled and plated the beans, and they were ’bout as hot as a November night, but she gave me the big plate. She really is sweet, my Lenore.

Now, lukewarm limas ain’t nothing to write home about, but for all the bad people can say ’bout Lenore, can’t nobody hold a candle to this woman’s work in the kitchen. I’m talkin’ roasted wild crow, plucked and buttered, stuffed with pickled acorns. Wild onions, with the roots still on the bulbs, little white fingers that tickle when you swallow ’em whole. Lenore’s biggest talent was taking the nothing, the absolute shit mounds around us, and turning them into magic. Into gold. That’s one reason I married her. And she wasn’t always so nutty. Not when I took her on. Had two good feet too. Her head got turnt backwards when our boy passed. Maybe both of ours did. She didn’t sleep any, neither. Up all hours whisperin’ to the damn housebugs.

After a good meal, there’s only one thing a man needs. I emptied myself into her, seed and soul. Afterwards, we lay on the sheetless mattress, good and sated, under the heap of blanket scraps and ashy smoke from the collection of cigarette stubs I saved for nights like these. Just enough puffs left on ’em to keep. I was too spent to get up, and the bed, naked as us, was a map of singed black holes and crusted white.

I shouldn’t have let in the passing thought from the day before, but it’s damn hard. I knew it’d come to haunt me that night, and it did, flames-a-lickin’.

Rex’s howl—he screamed like a dog when the heat was eatin’ him up. Aunt Sue—her body got all burnt, but the fire got put out before it reached her head. They found her with the plastic from her jockey lot necklace all shelled up on her neck and chest. Thank the good Lord, Lenore woke me before the dream kept going. At least I didn’t make it to the stables.

“Earlie! Oh, Earlie! Wake up. Wake UP! Don’t you know it’s a miracle!”

She was a spring bee, buzzin’ in short lines, back and forth, back and forth, in front of our mirror, the oversized shard damaged with black, mounted to the wall. She cupped her belly between her skinny arms.

“Earlie. It’s a baby. We’re having a baby!”

I stared at her from the mattress, half asleep.

“A baby, huh? I thought the midwife told you you couldn’t have no more.” She didn’t seem to hear me. “A baby,” she said. “We been gifted.”

“It didn’t happen that quick with . . .” I didn’t say his name.

The gap where his name wasn’t struck her a pause.

“Oh, Earlie, don’t be stupid. Of course it does. It always happens right when . . . it happens. We just didn’t know right when it happened before.”

“And you know that now?”

“Of course I do, Earlie, or I wouldn’t be fixin’ to make this feast, would I?”

“I s’pose not.”

“Well, don’t just lay in bed all day.” She fussed at the covers, so up I got. “And make yourself decent. We’re goin’ into town. I’ve been savin’ a good barter for times like this.”

She had on her special dress, the long green one, only a little brown-stained. She even had a hair clip in, her only one, bronze and rusted green, and shaped like a horse. She looked lovely as a spring lily.

“But how do you know this time?” I asked, brushing her stomach skin with my palm.

“A woman always knows after she felt it once.” Her eyes looked behind me instead of at me, even though there wasn’t nothin’ back there. “Plus, they told me.”

For a second, I was worried she was talking about the roaches again, but I noticed she was touching a photo. It was a photo of them. Of us. Our family, the Johnsons. Together in the flesh. My heart swelled. I kissed her hand.

“Course, baby, course. Let’s go get some fixins.”

Last time we went to town, Tom from Goods on Low wouldn’t even let us buy the shit in our cart. Said we were “welcome to come complete the purchase when we was wearing proper attire.” His eyes kept slidin’ down towards Lenore’s feet. It was the left one his eyes lasered in on. The fire turned it into somethin’ people didn’t like to look at and somethin’ that wouldn’t fit inside any shoes we’d found.

Today she’d wrapped up her damaged soldier, hidden it under the nice dress, and these piggies were off to market.

It was nice to be out with her, walking the long poppy-filled path to town. All kickin’ up dirt, dust, and smiles like we’re kids again, like we’re fuckin’ fourteen. It made me want to take her, fill her up right there, on the road to Tom’s, ’til I remembered that there was a baby inside her. Or she said so anyway. Her moon times had been late on occasion before. Either way, picturing a baby floating around in her belly aroused me a good deal less, and I was happy carrying on walking rather than putting any action towards the sex.

Goods on Low was in the same spot. When we went in, I didn’t see Tom. Instead, it was a town boy, sixteen, maybe seventeen. I contented myself with browsing the hardware selection while Lenore filled the cart. I like the hardware section. Stuff you can use, stuff a man could put to work in his life. And they made it pretty, too. Silver that looked so shiny you’d swear it was melted. Melted . . .

“Pa!” The funny thing about having a public breakdown is you kinda know it’s happenin’ but can’t stop it.

“Pa! Hey, come here!” I felt my side smash into Tom’s scuffed linoleum.

I moseyed into the stables. Guy was always in the stables.

“What is it?” I was thinking about the busted starter in my Ford. I was only half listening. He was asking to use somethin’ for a project, some dumb shit they were making him do at his school.

“Sure.”

And that’s the last thing I said to my boy. The last time I shoulda looked at him. The last time I didn’t listen.

I never could tell Lenore. She’d probably have forgiven me. Or maybe not. For fuck’s sake how many times had I told the boy not to play with Rex’s torch lighters?

Truth is, when you’ve got a kid crawling on you for your whole resting life, there tends to be a good bit of bullshitting attention. I’m ashamed to say that’s where I left it with Guy.

Pulling out of an episode feels like comin’ up from the bottom of a lake. Sounds gurgly too. I was just coming up for my first breath of air when Lenore reached the counter to pay. She was arguing with the town boy.

“No, I’m telling you, they’re genuine!”

“Ma’am, I, I can’t take those.” He took a step back.

Leave it to Tom to hire a fuckin’ softy town boy who couldn’t barter.

“What’s the matter, darlin’?” I asked, approaching the counter.

“She’s trying to pay with . . . with. She’s trying to pay with . . . teeth.”

I looked at what was in Lenore’s delicate hand. Guy’s jar of baby teeth. One of her most prized possessions. She’d kept them all, every one of them he’d left under the pillow.

“Ma’am, I said I can’t take that!” Standing that close to a lady brandishing a jar of human teeth had put some hot air in his gusset.

“Tom barters with us all the time,” Lenore said.

“Tom hasn’t been in for half a year. He lost his toe to gout, and I ain’t hardly seen him leave his couch since.”

“Well, Tom is still the owner of this here establishment, and he accepts barters. Says so on the sign.” She pointed.

“Tom ain’t takin’ no teeth.” I stepped between them.

“Lenore. You can’t use the teeth. You can’t give those away. Not for anything. Not for some food.” She looked at me. Our eyes locked a second, my dirt-brown and her lake-water hazel. Then, my sweet Lenore, she screamed and flipped the cart, spilling all the unpurchased ingredients. Oranges and herbs scattered into a line between me and the town boy.

“Shit.” He kicked an egg yolk off his shoe.

“Sorry. She’s, uh . . . with child.”

I left without cleaning the mess.

Lenore walked ahead of me on the way home; little puffs of dust rose from each of her right-footed stomps, parallel to the lined smudges of the left drag. She went straight into foraging. She didn’t even look back at me as she disappeared into the brush.

My dreams were all mixed up that night. The town boy’s face, smeared with judgment and disgust, as Lenore shook a jar of teeth at him, pleading. Cans of piss overflowed on the dirty ground, roaches scuttling past, not regular ones but jumbo, the size of big dogs or little kids. They whispered to me. Only I couldn’t understand what the hell they were sayin’. And the stables. A view of the stables from behind, black smoke and bright flame. The stench of burning flesh is worse when you know it’s your own kin. It’s the aroma of what you’d smell like, your cells and hair and bones, if they were on fire.

When I woke up, our shit-hole house was a new place. I almost thought I was still dreamin’, except the roaches crowding near the piss pots were regular-sized. She’d moved the old flimsy barn door that had fallen off its hinges. And my Lenore, my darlin’ Lenore, with her womanly touch, had turned it into a table, raised up with big cans and old cinder blocks. She’d even laid a tablecloth over the top of it, Guy’s old baby blanket.

It was one of the only things that survived the fire. He’d left it outside near the big oak the morning of. He and Lenore had been sitting on top of it, eating wild blueberries. There were still little purple stains near the fading horses at the edges, little cartoons blotted with purple like their guts were fallin’ out.

That was about all of the blanket you could see. The rest was covered.

I admired the baskets filled with chickweed and pawpaw, with the little yellow sunshine heads of dandelions poking up through the sides.

My eyes roamed over to a roasted sow—a mother, frozen in roasted time with several of its babes forever attached at the teat. She’d put little sprigs of parsley and wild onions in mama’s mouth rather than the typical apple you might see at Puerto Rican barbecues near town.

We didn’t have no pigs, nor did it look like she caught them wild—they weren’t turned; their skin was crisp but baby pink, soft-lookin’. She must have snuck up to Flawson’s Farm in the night.

Now, Lenore wasn’t no thief. But she also wasn’t above doin’ what needed doin’ when it needed doin’.

It looked like she might have gone farther out than Flawson’s. There was a pot of rattlesnake beans, long-podded, the purple stripes cooked out. They looked like the ones old Millie Mae grew down at the North End. There were other signs of Millie Mae’s produce on the table, too—long, pointed red okras. They were seeping slime the way okra does—thick green puddles under the curled, seedy fingers.

“Well,” she said. Her eyes were on me, hard and squinty, like they get sometimes when she expects somethin’.

“Baby! This looks amazing.” I slid my legs into my long johns, eager to reach the table.

“Oh no, you don’t!” she said.

“What? I’m starving.” She had her arm out blocking me, and I carved around her both ways, eager as a mosquito.

“Earl, no! Don’t you touch a thing. We’re waitin’.”

“Waitin’? What are we waitin’ for? Be a crime to let it get cold?”

She rushed around, grabbing four mismatched pieces of our clunkier furniture and our one real chair—one of those plastic numbers they keep in tall stacks out by the side of junk stores—and set them around the table while keepin’ a devil’s eye on me.

“Who did you invite? Is it . . . Millie?” I asked, glancing at the okra.

“Millie?” She whacked me one across the forehead. “Earlie, who do you think this feast is for?”

“I guess for us on account of the new baby.” She looked at me like I’d said to put syrup in the tractor fuel tank.

“It’s for them. They’re coming.” She was looking at the mirror shard.

“Them?” I asked.

“They didn’t talk to you, Earl. They know you ain’t like that. I listen. I’ve always had a way with those sorts of things.”

“What sorts of things? Who didn’t talk to me? The roaches?” This wasn’t it. She rolled her eyes.

“Spirits and that.”

I couldn’t get to what she was sayin’. Then I counted the chairs she’d brought up to the table. Five chairs. The exact right number for a Johnson family reunion. Except our family was dead, all burned up.

“Lenore, they’re gone. There was a fire.”

“I know that!” she said. “And like I said, spirits and that. They’re coming back, Earlie. They want to be here for us, bless the new baby.”

“He ain’t even here yet.”

“She doesn’t need to be here to get blessed, Earl.”

“Who told you they were comin’?” I asked, even though she’d clearly gone full-in, crazy wise.

“They told me in the night.”

“Who? Lenore, the fuckin’ roaches did not tell you our dead family is comin’. Baby, I’m sorry, but I can’t let you carry on.” Usually, I coddled her, tender to her oddities. But this tugged at somethin’ in my gut.

“Yeah, Earl?” Her typically sugared voice had a sour cut around the edges. “That ain’t all they told me about. They said they know about you . . . and that day.” She rushed out the door, leaving me with a long john up one leg and a ball of rotten in my belly. I didn’t touch the food.

“Pa! Hey, Pa, come here.” He was up in the rafters of the stables, where we kept the extra bales of hay. The windy week prior made a mess of the yard. Straw strewn every which way, some trees uprooted, even some chickens tumbled down the road towards Flawson’s. We tried raking up the straw; there was enough of it around to rig a makeshift bale or two. We stored them up in the old wood box in the stable rafters.

But the gas keep. Me and Rex built her back when the land was younger. The official ones, the big steel soldiers, cost more than we had. So we built our own, hiding it in the barn, because who the hell were they to tell us how to build on our land.

In all the storm trouble, one of the goats had gotten into the gas keep. She was going crazy, buckin’ around and shittin’. I knocked over a few fuel bins trying to get her to settle, and the ground was soaked with kerosene.

The grounds around the barn.

The straw on the grounds.

The straw blown clear up against the house.

And the straw stored in the stables.

It was cartoon-like, the whoosh that overtook him. I didn’t see the smile leave his face, the look of delight from finally getting a successful light from Rex’s torch. The smoke and flames were too thick. It ate the old wood box stuffed with fuel-soaked straw and my boy quicker than I could reach him. Quicker than I could understand what was happening.

Guy gone, I only wanted one thing: to save Lenore. I ignored Rex’s screams and Sue’s calls for help. Ran right past them. They’d been window washing in the foyer. The fire liked whatever Sue’d concocted for a cleaner. When I found her, Lenore was trapped under a fallen cabinet, the flames eating their way up one foot. By the time I’d dragged her outside and tried to go back in to help them, Rex had gone silent, and Sue—Sue was all burnt up from the tits down and melted in her necklace.

It was all chalked up to an accident, legally, but on account of negligence we didn’t get no insurance money. A couple of times, I almost told her, my Lenore. I’d feel the words in my mouth, but I swallowed them down. She was the only thing left. She had to stay.

I sat. The feast sat. Lenore paced. The roaches scuttled. She wasn’t bothered on conversation, seeing as how we left things last and I wasn’t keen to push her. At last, she settled. She sat across from me. I gazed around before my eyes stopped on her. She opened her mouth but shut it again, and I wanted her to yell at me, hate me, anything. But she just shook her head, one turn to the left and one turn to the right, and nothing in her expression. The sun moved out of the sky, staying a second on Lenore, her face and her belly. Then the dark moved in. If we had a clock, it would have ticked a thousand times. Maybe we’d have one of those with the tiny bird who jumped out. Cuckoo. Cuckoo. In the thick of the feast smells, I caught somethin’ else, a smoky, cloying rot, and it stuck in my throat. Cuckoo. Cuckoo. CUCKOO.

Then, they were there.

The chairs filled with bodies that were more solid than I’d imagined.

All but one. Where was he?

“Lenore! Earl. My God, it’s been too long. What’s it been? Twenty moons?” It was Sue. One moment, nothing, and the next, she was there, stuffing her face with pickled parsnips. “Is that my horse pin?” She reached to Lenore’s hair and took the pin out to examine it.

“It’s been since the fire,” Rex said, filling his plate. “And this fucker passed us up, didn’t he? Ran right past.” Rex was the same as always. He laughed his big laugh.

“It’s still got the garnet eyes,” Sue said, fingering the little horse’s face. Lenore showed no sign of taking any of it in. Not even with a god damn ghost’s arm in her face. She just stared. Stared at the empty seat.

“Oh honey,” Sue drawled, mouth full. “I don’t think he’ll be able to make it. Lenore, I’m so sorry, darlin’.”

Lenore blinked fast.

“No, don’t cry now,” she soothed, offering her food-covered napkin. “It wasn’t you. He was hoppin’ out of his skin with excitement when he heard we was comin’. And he misses you too. Even you, Earl.”

“But the burns—the boy won’t show face because of the burns,” Rex said. “Stays cooped up like he did here. Stable suited him then. I reckon it suits him now.” The talk of stables put a heat up my neck.

I looked at Rex, and I saw he wasn’t how he’d always been. Faint red marks showed all over his arms, between his tattoos, on his face. Rex fingered the spot where my eyes lay.

“Yeah, ours healed up pretty good. You can still see them if you look close, but your boy—he wasn’t so lucky.”

Sue tapped her melted chest plate.

“And why is that, Earl?” Her face had turned nasty. “What did you do, Earl?”

“I didn’t. I didn’t do nothin’!”

“Liar!” Rex yelled.

“Liar! Liar! Liar!” Sue screamed.

“LIAR.” A chorus of roaches echoed the proclamation.

Lenore continued to stare, clutching her gut and face picked cotton-white.

“No!” I yelled.

The table began to shake. The plattered sow, eyes bulging and orifices still stuffed, rolled in her bed of greens. The piglets wriggled and squealed. The okra grew gray, then black, and then white and wormed. The tablecloth—Guy’s blanket—lit up slow at the corner, a line of orange climbing the fabric, turning the little gutted horses to dust. A writhing, rotting dance and the smoke-thick air stinking of roaches, piss, and decayed relatives. Then, in a cough of orange, flames ate up the feast, and all of us with it, whole.

A roach crawled across my cheek, waking me. Feeling like a fly on a strip of goo, I unstuck the other side of my face from the table.

A table. There was a table.

It wasn’t all burned.

Guy’s blanket splayed under the feast’s remains. The food was the only thing wrecked, all strewn across the table and half-eaten. Lenore was sleeping in her chair, her bum leg still wrapped up from the trip to town.

“Baby. Baby, time to get up.”

She didn’t move.

“Baby,” I said again. She was always such a light sleeper. My heart took on double time in my chest. What if this was it, my punishment? What if they came and they took Lenore?

“BABY!” I yelled, jumping up to shake her.

She uncurled slow from sleep and looked up at me, still half in it.

“What’s wrong?” She rubbed her eyes, then looked down at the table.

“Earl! I told you not to touch anything. You can’t even keep your hands off for one night.”

“Baby, it wasn’t me, it was—”

“Earl, you can’t lie your way out of this one.” She looked at me, pupil to pupil, and squinted.

Lie. Liar? Did she remember or didn’t she?

After a while, she said, “I guess they didn’t come. Maybe we was wrong about the baby too.” I didn’t know what to say. She was supposed to be the loopy one.

“Where’s your horse pin?” I asked her. She fingered her hair.

“Guess I lost it out in the woods.”

“You had it when we sat down.”

“I don’t know, Earl. I’ll find it if it’s here. Not now, I’m feelin’ ill.” She cupped her stomach down low near her hip. She headed to the washroom. I just stood there staring at it all. The dregs of the feast, muddled and buggy, and the now empty chairs.

And there it was, a splotch of red on the seat of Lenore’s white plastic chair. I walked over to it and ran my fingers across it. Thicker than water. It was blood. I rubbed it between my index finger and thumb, and on the second swipe, I think it turned to ash.

pieces.html:
At the grocery store my son asks
why the lobsters’ claws are taped shut.

So they don’t hurt each other, I say.

He considers this from the cart.

Then why are they together?

The man behind the seafood counter
looks up from wrapping haddock.

Nobody answers.

One lobster climbs over another,
gets halfway up the glass,
slides backward.

My son wants to know
which one we’re taking home.

None of them.

He asks why they’re here.

For people to buy.

Why?

To eat.

He looks at the tank.

The seafood man turns on the faucet
and rinses his knife.

At checkout my son asks
if the lobsters know.

Know what?

That somebody gets to pick.

I put the milk on the belt.
Then the eggs.
Then the chicken.

He reaches from the cart
and turns the chicken
label-side down.

pieces.html: Akash wrote to say he’d made it to our Motherland, that the first person he saw was the Queen. She was eating Quality Street from a golden cup. Akash said she offered him the one in the emerald wrapper even though he’d actually wanted the amethyst one but boys from the colony (his words) could not ask the Queen for such things so he took the green gem, swallowed it whole, and asked her what next. The Queen blinked. Akash asked her if she didn’t mind loaning him some of her jewels, she had so many. She gave him three diamond-encrusted platinum batons. He mailed a photo of himself in a loincloth, posing with his gifts, looking like Shah Jahan. His mother asked, but will he send us any real money. Ten years later, Akash returned to the village. He told us he’d accidentally left the batons on the plane. We took him through the front door, then the kitchen, and showed him his mother, lying on the ground like a peaceful prune. Akash said it was a shame his Amma never got to meet the Queen, she really was a lovely lady. In two days, Akash was back in his Motherland and we never saw him again. Someone’s cousin told us he had turned himself into a turbaned Guru and many fair-skinned women sat around him, their eyes closed, chanting Our King, Our King. At least he finally succeeded.

pieces.html:
It isn’t a bird
perched on top
of the square fence post.

It’s too still
and too dark.

It’s a shadow
or a ghost.

But he doesn’t believe me,
just as he never believes
any fact I tell him
from before he was born
which makes every word bitter.
It’s not a bird, I say, bitterly,
but I don’t hold him back

when he runs straight at the post,
trying to make a shadow fly.

pieces.html:
If the metro made Pat especially misanthropic, it was primarily because of what she did and didn’t overhear there. On the street people rubbed the odd spark off one another in passing or blathered the occasional bit of nonsense or near-nonsense to one another over alcohol—but sitting and standing on metro trains they were looking at their smartphones, having conversations whose interlocutors would, in a transcript, have been impossible to tell apart, or, at best, looking into space. They weren’t even interested-and-so-interesting enough to steal glances at one another (you could forget about ogling!), or to look out the window when the train was going overground. Indeed, the conversations they had were, in most cases, part and parcel of this “not looking.” Old-style small talk still occurred, of course—but it was rapidly losing ground to a mode of communication which made “polite meaningless words” seem as quaintly desirable as, say, listening to an album all the way through or knowing the names of the six or seven species of bird you came across regularly.

“Serial me-ing” she called this increasingly preponderant way of conversing. Although it could be taken to different levels and in various directions, all it essentially consisted of was two or more people saying “I’m here” by turns. A group of university students, for example, would be caught (by Pat) taking turns as follows:

. . . “I got a 5 but I didn’t study.”

“I persuaded the teacher to give me a 10 so as to keep my average up.”

“None of my teachers would do that.”

“I’ve got a resit tomorrow” . . .

Or two forty-somethings, we-ing rather than me-ing by virtue of their respective joint bank accounts, would be tuned in on as they “dirtied the airwaves” with the likes of:

. . . “We’re going on a Baltic cruise.”

“That’s nice. We’re going to Berlin.”

“Oh, we went to Berlin two years ago. You’ll love it. But I told you about it, didn’t I? Anyway, next year we’ve decided we’re finally going to Argentina.”

“Lucky you. We’ve always wanted to go there” . . .

So boring were they, these “conversations,” that after about ten seconds of listening to one of them, she was anaesthetised to the point where not even the compensatory pleasure of feeling superior was available to her.

When Pat was on the metro she (a) always stood—even when the carriage was empty—and (b) did one of five things: either she listened in (and regretted it); or she looked for—and occasionally found—more or less interesting-seeming people within eyeshot; or she looked out the window (or at her own reflection); or, having called them all a bunch of letzten Menschen, she proceeded to toy with them, looking, for example, at the trainers they were wearing (she always wore boots) and anywhere between gleefully and wearily staging a little three-way quantic snail race, which she kept going (and sometimes even propelled to a finish) by three-handedly counting them forward as now Nike, now Adidas, and now Other; or—as she was doing at that moment, on the morning of the day she would die of a brain haemorrhage—she moved so deeply in thought that if she never missed her station, it must have been by virtue of some sort of “waking-just-before-the-alarm-goes-off” mechanism or, why not, psychism.

The thought or thought-system she was moving in right now—a moment before somebody said her name and made her come to with a start—was that of her money problems and what miracles might get her out of them. If one of the miracles considered was death—and death, moreover, not by suicide but by precisely the kind of major biological blowout which would, in fact, put an end to her that very same day—then there was nothing prescient, coincidental, or even surprising about this. Pat not only thought about death often but enjoyed doing so, thinking-about-death being, for her, akin (she imagined) to what thinking-about-retirement was for the death-blind letzte Mensch.

But at the moment when somebody said her name (as if from within the body of her thoughts), Pat had moved out of the valley of death and into the far less agreeable, indeed, wholly disagreeable brown-and-beige-Möbius-strip-like series of interiors of having to live (possibly) with her parents. Thus, despite its making her jump, this interruption was as agreeable to Pat as, say, finding ten or, rather, five or, anyway, two euros under the bed would have been.

Pat looked up and to her right—and saw Elly standing there holding one of the floor-to-roof steel bars as if it were a staff of power or something. Good old Elly! She was, needless to say, as gently smiling, frailly beautiful, and doe-eyed as ever. Only, on this occasion, with that staff of power preternaturalising her frailty and with those letzten Menschen contrasting her spirituality, she evinced something which for Pat was new: a sort of shining elfinness—one that made a supra-Elly of her.

“Hello, Elly,” said Pat beaming pleasure at her. “What are you doing here? Visiting your sisters?”

“I’m back living here now,” she said with that slow liquid contralto of hers. “I have been for about six months. What about you? Are you still single-handedly making a Bohemia of Paterna?”

“Yeah, yeah, yeah,” said Pat not wanting to talk about it. “Or in a word: yeah. But so, anyway, what, you’ve been transferred to a hospital here, have you?”

“No, I still work in Requena. I spend two hours a day driving there and back. But it was time for Juan and I to finally start cohabiting. We’ve been together for twelve years now.”

“I’m glad you’re taking things so slowly. At that rate you’ll die at a ripe old age without having got far enough down the line to see the essential horror of human existence.”

“I’d like to think so,” said Elly in a way which, despite her smile, seemed to indicate that that was indeed her intention.

“And you’re still A-&-E-ing it up there, are you? Or have they put you out to pasture at a health centre?”

“No, I’m not burnt out yet,” laughed Elly. “In fact, I might even be becoming fireproof.”

“And how many die on you a week?” Pat wanted to know with an impetus that easily got her, post-utterance, beyond a couple of disapproving comments and some looking askance which she heard and glimpsed coming from the letzten Menschen.

“About three on average,” laughed Elly, God bless her (although, of course, she can afford to laugh at my flippancy, thought Pat—because it isn’t her doing).

“And how’s your relationship with death going? Are you traumatised and taking something, positively revelling in it, or have you become callous?”

“The third,” she limited herself to answering—although, being Elly, she’d laughed again, and was even now continuing to bathe Pat in smiling, doe-eyed goodwill.

But Pat had picked up more than a couple of comments from “the audience” that time, and, irritated-going-on-pissed-off all of a sudden, she rapidly told Elly, “Yeah, you said about becoming fireproof,” then turned her head and gaze to the left—and immediately encountered the trouble she was after: a pair of fifty-something-year-old female eyes looking daggers at her. Pat’s first reaction was to look away—but then, given a shove back into the ring by her own irritation, and having, she hoped, succeeded in turning that initial movement towards flight into what appeared a flurry of blinks, she went on to do what, as she did it, converted her mounting anger into a loud, more-than-a-little maniacal internal laugh: staring straight back at the woman’s daggers, she opened her own eyes as wide (literally) as she could and . . . made the woman look away.

The woman, it’s true, let off a Parthian “Lunatic” as she came scrambling down off her redoubt—but Pat simply took that as the compliment it undoubtedly essentially was.

For a moment, she was very much ready for the next one—very much tempted, that was, to look further left and so take on the next “fucker.” But then an absurd vision of it actually coming to blows interceded (since, whatever else happened, she wasn’t going to descend to arguing with them), and seeing herself knocking them around and down with the martial arts skills she in no way possessed, she turned back to Elly with such a broad smile on her face that the corners of Elly’s mirror smile seemed to go up past the tip of her nose.

“Well,” said Pat. “We’ve only got a couple of stations left. So you’d better hurry up and tell me first about your family and then about the mad dogs and comatose cats which, your family being your family, are almost certainly lying somewhere within its folds.”

As she strode uphill from the station to her brother’s flat, Pat was giving herself what, friendliness of tone notwithstanding, amounted to a talking-to.

It’s not as if I’m the Grim Reaper’s next-door neighbour, whom he regularly borrows sugar from, she was telling herself as part of a “necessary,” self-prescribed coming-back-down-to-earth process after her “exploit” on the metro. Yes, she thought, they’re death-blind, but—

But what? she demanded suddenly, unable to take “this shit” even from herself. They fucking started it!

And she would undoubtedly have been punished for her “heroic victory” qua hubris with a nice little, tight little anxiety-generating circle of Hell on earth if, just then, a big ginger tom hadn’t appeared.

He was sauntering down the middle of the street, holding his tail up as though the slight effort that required had been the essence of play and so art. Having become inwardly silent at the sight of him, Pat nodded him a wordless hello. He, for his part, not only regarded her face toward face, but continued to do so. Thus, turning his head as they drew closer and closer to the line beyond which—she on the pavement and he in the middle of the road—they’d walk and saunter into one another’s pasts, he gave her back far more than she’d given him.

Sufficient happiness, she would, perhaps, have called what he gave her if she hadn’t still been mute inside at the moment when she felt it most.

Only, when she and he had, in fact, already crossed said “line,” and Pat, picturing the intercom panel to herself, was beginning (with reemergent language) to try to pre-work-out which of the innumerable unmarked buzzers her brother’s was, she suddenly decided to look back over her shoulder—in order to see what the ginger tom was doing now.

What he was doing was two things: sauntering down the middle of the street and looking over his shoulder at Pat.

pieces.title: Mirror
pieces.author: William Garvey
pieces.html:
I adjust the bicycle mirror
to see what I’ve left behind.
The dog walker tethered
to three curly-haired canines
whose breed names end with doodle.
The four-wheeler racing by
the old guy in a Blue Jays cap.
It rouses a cloud of crusher dust
he sweeps from his face.
With the same hand he expresses
his feelings for the driver.
My wife and me enjoying
mint tea on the porch caught up
in plans and then my father,
withered, rising painfully from bed.
My brother in the aisle
of a local hardware store
inspecting the strengths of rope.
I stop looking.

pieces.html: That bell that bell that goddamned bell. You know the one? The one that the victors ring on their way out—after their last treatment. The center is so quiet, the voices hushed. The bell is so loud. Clang-clang-clang and cheers of wild joy. “Does it make me a bad person?” she asks, licking her shriveled-up lips. “That I cannot stand that bell?” “No,” I say. Because I, too, hate that goddamned bell, and I’m not a bad person. Just a person. “Fuck that bell,” I say. “Fuck it,” she repeats. I know, and she knows, that forever, if I ever hear another bell, any kind of bell, something will bloom open in my stomach, and I’ll think of her, nestled right here, tucked under her fuzzy blue blanket, and I’ll whisper, “Fuck that bell,” just in case she can hear.

pieces.title: Our Daughter Haunts Us Now
pieces.author: Cecil Morris
pieces.html:
Our daughter, dead now five years,
returned this Día de los Muertos
even though we are not Hispanic
or Latinx or religious believers
in anything beyond the light
and dark of this world, the now
and its relentless presence,
even though we built no altar,
made no ofrenda of favored foods
like caramel-dipped apples
or chilled white cake with strawberry-
infused buttercream frosting
and crown of glazed strawberries.
She did, our daughter, come back.
She lives now in the garage fridge,
the ancient one passed down to us
from my mother, the one silent
in its cold offices for years
and years. Now, when we are out there
shifting boxes or hunting tools,
we hear from that antique fridge
the sounds of our daughter slamming
her door or breaking dishes
in the kitchen as she did
whenever it was her turn
to wash. Sometimes we can hear
the grumbling of eternal
dissatisfaction or the breathy sigh
of her favorite too revealing dress
or the thunder of her feet.
We look inside the fridge. The light
still works and everything is cold.

pieces.html:
Ava glides over the polished floorboards of her sixth-floor Flatbush apartment to the music of the New York Philharmonic performing a Strauss waltz. Her satin-and-suede dance shoes hardly make a sound. With eyes closed, her hands grasp an imaginary partner that she changes every few days depending on who she sees in real life—always a handsome man that she mentally dresses in nineteenth-century evening attire.

A loud knock on her door brings her back from her dream of whirling couples in a Viennese ballroom. She squints through the door’s peephole. A stout middle-aged woman, barely tall enough to be seen, stands in the hallway. Ava slides two bolts back, twists the deadbolt, and opens the door on the chain.

“Yes, Mrs. Lanchart?”

“I’m sorry, Ava, but you’re playing that music too loud again. Would you please turn it down?”

“I’m sorry, Mrs. Lanchart, I keep forgetting where I am.”

“Why do you play that old music, anyway? With the boys back from Vietnam, the bands are playing hot stuff in the clubs. You should come with Harold and me . . . get out of that damn apartment for a change.”

“Thanks for the offer, but I’m too tired after work.”

“You’re not working Saturdays.”

“Thanks again for the offer. I’ll turn the music down.”

Ava smiles through the narrow opening, knowing Mrs. Lanchart means well. Her neighbor just shakes her head and retreats. Ava shudders at the thought of visiting a smoke-filled nightclub where the music’s so loud you can’t hold a conversation, not that she has much to say. She moves to the stereo that has quieted on its own. Turning the LP over, Ava cues the needle and lowers the volume. Everyone has a different tolerance for sound, and Mrs. Lanchart is her most sensitive neighbor so far.

The Blue Danube flows from the stereo’s speakers. Ava continues to waltz—one-two-three, one-two-three—her willowy body barely disturbing the moist winter air. The heat radiators cough, ostensibly in time with the music. After an hour of dancing she returns from Vienna to her walkup apartment in Flatbush, to 1973 and her job as a junior accountant with one of New York City’s largest law firms. She dabs at her glistening face with a towel, sips a glass of Riesling, and remembers back a decade.

“So what are you gonna do after we graduate?” Emily, Ava’s only high-school friend, asked.

“Haven’t you heard? I’ve been accepted at Columbia.”

“How the hell can your parents afford that? Your Pop must be doin’ a whole bunch of engine rebuilds.”

“I received a scholarship and I’ve saved money from working at my uncle’s bodega.”

“Lucky damn you. Meanwhile, I’ll be waitressing for the rest of my life.”

“Don’t say that, Em. Something will come your way.”

“Yeah, I just hope he’s handsome and rich . . . well, at least rich.”

The girls had laughed.

Emily asked, “So what are you gonna take for sixth period elective?”

“I don’t know. I might take ballroom dancing from Mrs. Flanalle.”

“What for?”

“There may be boys there. I might actually get to . . . you know, touch one.”

Emily giggled. “Oh you’ll touch one all right. I took that class at the end of sophomore year. I had enough boys stomp on my feet to last a lifetime. And all they really wanted to do was crunch my boobs.”

“I won’t have that problem,” Ava said and frowned.

“Hey, hey. It’ll be fun. Enjoy it. It’ll probably be the only time you’ll do ballroom dancing, until you’re gray-haired and they pair you with some old geezer at the rest home.”

“I’m already feeling old.”

“Not hardly.”

Ava reported to the gymnasium for the first dance class. Fourteen other kids had also signed up. With eleven girls and four boys, Ava did most of her dancing with girls, each struggling to decide who should lead and who should follow. The dance music in four-four time seemed jarring to Ava. Only the waltz rhythms seemed to fit, let her glide with the music and whirl and whirl around the gym until her partners complained about getting dizzy. Ava thought, Maybe that’s why those Viennese liked it so much, it was a type of drug for them. It would become one for Ava.

In her senior year at Columbia, with a job already lined up, she moved into her Flatbush apartment, over the objections of her mother.

“You don’t have to live alone and pay rent,” her mother reasoned. “You can stay with us.”

“Mom, I’m twenty-two. Aren’t you sick of me being around? You and Pop deserve your own space.”

Her mother grinned. “Yes, you can be a pain sometimes . . . but not all the time.”

“Well, now’s your chance to do all those fun things and get the heck out of Brooklyn. I’ll be paying my own way from here on out.”

“You’ll probably make more than your father . . . but don’t ever tell him that.”

“Don’t worry, I won’t.”

Ava was glad that her mom had not bugged her about meeting men and getting married. She would not miss those embarrassing moments. Long ago she’d realized that her mother’s compliments about her grace and beauty had no relationship to the angular face and skeletal body that she stared at every morning in the mirror.

Her father helped her move in. But she stopped him after the second time he climbed six flights of stairs and looked ready to pass out. Her cousin from Jersey hauled most of the stuff upstairs on the promise that she’d buy him a case of Ballantine when they finished. Ava brought her own bed and dressers that she commandeered from her parents’ place. The apartment included some usable furniture and an old ratty rug that covered the living room floor. The rug had to go.

With much effort she pried open the window that overlooked the narrow light well. Far below, cardboard boxes, broken furniture, and even a mattress or two littered the snowy ground. Ava rolled up the rug, hauled it to the window, and shoved it foot-by-foot through the opening. It unraveled on the way down, looking like some pirate’s sail, folding and flapping in the frigid wind. That first dusk she stared wide-eyed as a homeless woman staggered into the jumble of junk from the alley and covered herself with the rug. In the morning deep snow hid everything, as if the trash and the woman didn’t exist. Ava shuddered to think what the building’s Super might find come spring.

Ava found a small-time contractor to refinish the living room’s hardwood floor to a smooth glistening surface. When complete, she began her ritual of waltzing, three or four nights a week. As the country struggled to find its way out of Vietnam, as young men disappeared from the neighborhoods, as college hippies and yippies railed against The Establishment, as teargas became a known stench, as the military-industrial complex spun out of control, Ava danced.

She’d wear a simple flared skirt, drink a glass or two of wine after supper, watch the outside world’s turmoil on TV, then turn off all of the lights except for one, and waltz. Afterward, excited, her nerves buzzing, she’d shower and go to bed, touching herself, but not too much, not wanting to degrade herself or lose the mental images of dancers in huge ballrooms, of gallant men in dark evening dress, the women in long full gowns, all whirling, whirling. The dance got her there.

Every weekday morning, Ava takes the subway from Flatbush to Midtown Manhattan and her twelfth-floor office. She’s been with the law firm now for thirty years, a competent accountant, having mastered the new computer technologies, and being promoted to section manager, in charge of budgeting. Her work relationships are all business, and although Ava gets lost in the numbers, she finds her co-workers colorless and uninteresting. She suspects they feel the same about her.

In 1996 Ava’s father dies of a massive stroke and her mother prepares to move upstate to live with her younger sister in Utica . . . but not before criticizing Ava one last time.

“Jesus, Ava, you make good money and you’re still living in that dump. You could afford a Fifth Avenue apartment if you wanted.”

“Why would I move? You’ve lived in the same house with Pop even longer. Why didn’t you move?”

“We liked our neighbors and people knew us there, looked after your father and me when we needed help. You don’t know anybody, including your neighbors. And you never have anybody over, never—”

“Don’t start, Mother. I have what I need.”

“You mean that dance floor for one?”

“I like it like that. It’s uncomplicated and I can think whatever I want while dancing. Besides, it’s good exercise.”

Her mother grins. “I’ll give you that. You’re as skinny as ever, could pass for a twelve-year-old boy.”

“Thanks, Mom, for supporting my femininity.”

“For Christ sake, Ava, you live in a city with more than seven million people and you can’t find a single friend? What about the lady next door, Mrs. Lanchart?”

“Mom, she moved out over ten years ago. Besides, she always complained about the music.”

“I just don’t want you to give up, honey. You’re a nice person that should be with someone nice.”

“Yes, well, enjoy your train ride to Utica. Call me when you get there. I’d love to come up and visit you and Aunt Rose once you get settled.”

Ava never gets the chance. Within three weeks her mother suffers heart failure and dies within hours. Ava arranges for her to be shipped to NYC and buried in Green-Wood Cemetery, the same plot as her father and close to the grave of her Jersey cousin—killed in a car crash while driving drunk. Her parents had paid for their plot years before. It can hold one more casket.

Her office mates express their sympathy, but it all feels like empty words. She’s been alone most of her life and is satisfied with that—at least she thinks she is.

Years pass. Ava’s auburn hair turns gray, then white. She buys a CD player then a laptop computer to play MP3 files through her speaker system that now includes quadraphonic sound. In her mid-sixties, she wraps her knees in Ace bandages before dancing and downs a Vicodin with her first glass of Riesling. The pain is bearable but it interrupts her daydreaming. She fears the time when she may have to stop and figures that’s when she’ll follow that old ratty rug out the window and add herself to the trash heap below. There were rumors that Mrs. Lanchart’s husband, Harold, did that before she moved away.

At work, Ava slows down and her bosses notice. She’s forced to take the place of a more recent hire and is tasked again with basic accounting, under a younger person’s supervision. Because of the demotion, they expect her to quit. But to their surprise, she settles in and does excellent work, giving them no reason for termination.

One night, after listening to TV news, she sips wine and prepares to dance. There’s a knock on the door, the first in a long while. Through the peephole she sees a thick-bodied man wearing glasses, with thinning dark hair and large earlobes.

“What do you want?” she calls through the door.

“Sorry to bother you, miss. You don’t know me but can I talk with you for a minute?”

“What about?”

“Your dancing.”

Ava steps back from the door. “How . . . how do you know about that?”

“I live across the light well from you. My apartment is also on the sixth floor and . . . and I can see you spin and whirl.”

“What are you, some kind of creep? A Peeping Tom?”

“No, no. Please, I mean you no disrespect. But you must know that you are a wonderful dancer, so graceful, so full of life. I’ve been watching you on Tuesdays when I’m not working the night shift at the furniture factory.”

“Why would you do that?”

“I’m not sure. I . . . I guess I need something beautiful in my life. I’ve been alone for years . . . just like you . . . have lived in this complex since ’75.”

The silence builds between them. “So . . . so what do you want?” Ava asks.

“I thought maybe we could talk and . . . and if you wouldn’t mind, let me watch you dance.”

“Look, bud, I’m not some kind of freak show for you to ogle.”

“On . . . on my word . . . I want nothing like that.”

“What’s your name?”

“Aaron Moskowitz. And yours?”

“Ava.”

“I’m glad to finally meet you, Ava. I’m kind of . . . shy.”

“Wait just a moment.”

Ava bows her head and thinks about risks and benefits. She remembers why she took that dance class the last term in high school. She wonders if she’s still looking for physical and emotional connections, so many years later? Has all desire dried up and turned as white as her hair?

Ava unlocks the door, opens it on the chain, and stares at Aaron. He smiles at her, showing off gold crowns in a broad thick-lipped mouth.

“Come back next Tuesday at eight, Aaron. And bring a bottle of chilled Riesling.”

“Any . . . any particular brand or year?”

“No, but choose wisely.”

“I have . . . and have fun checking me out online.”

“I will. Us spinsters must be extra careful.”

“Well . . . you sure can spin.”

Aaron turns and disappears from view. Ava locks the door and sits on her sofa, heart racing. She wonders why. The guy is anything but handsome and probably as graceful as a rhino. She stares around the room, sniffs the air, moves to the hall mirror, and studies her gaunt reflection, her mind in scramble mode, trying to decide what to wear, how to clean the front room and bathroom, what wine glasses to set out, what music to play. Is she really going to meet this stranger? Why the hell not, she knows where he lives and his name. Not much risk. But still . . . maybe I should buy a gun?

Ava hurries to her window and looks across the courtyard to his dark apartment. As she watches, a light switches on and a hulking form moves behind see-through curtains. Her own window shade has been gone for years. Was that an unconscious act? Or was it an invitation? She smiles to herself, feeling the tingle of adventure touch her for the first time in a very long while.

Aaron Moskowitz freaks out. He wonders who that brave man was who crept along the hallways, knocked on that woman’s door, and asked if he could watch her dance. Who does that? Thinking about it now, he rushes to his apartment’s medicine cabinet and downs three antacids. But his mind continues to spin. He’ll ask Emilio at the market what Riesling is best. He’ll have his dark suit dry-cleaned and his Florsheims polished. The rest he can’t do much about; he hasn’t tried for years.

Aaron remembers summer nights when he would watch the lights in the apartment across the light well blink on. He’d open his window to hear the faint strains of music flowing from the woman’s apartment. He knew, even at first, that she listened and danced to waltzes.

The day after they met, Aaron goes online and reads up on any subject related to the waltz. He even tries to follow a simple dance lesson video that someone posted on Facebook. He doesn’t want Ava to think he’s stupid or ignorant. He scrubs hard at his stained and paint-encrusted hands, trying to remove the grunge from under his nails. He feels like a post-bar mitzvah teen waking up to the electric energy of sex and adulthood.

At precisely eight p.m. on Tuesday, Aaron stands outside Ava’s door and knocks—not a hammering knock, or a timid one, but something he hopes shows confidence, even though he has none. Bolts slide, chains rattle, and her door opens.

“Come in . . . Aaron.”

“Thank you. I . . . I hope this is okay.” He hands her the bottle of chilled Riesling.

“I’m sure it will be fine.”

Ava wears a simple flared skirt, no jewelry or makeup, hair put up in a bun that’s pulled so tight that it looks painful to endure. Her knees are wrapped in skin-colored bandages and she wears a well-worn pair of shoes.

“You . . . you look nice, Ava,” he murmurs.

She colors slightly and nods.

“Can I pour the wine for us?” he asks.

Again, just a nod. She motions to the sofa and coffee table where two long-stemmed wine glasses and a corkscrew rest. Aaron de-corks the bottle with a flair and pours the Riesling. Ava’s first sip almost empties the glass.

She laughs. “I’m . . . I’m sorry, I haven’t had a drink with anyone since college. And never here in this apartment.”

“I’ve been drinking alone for a long time too. Not something I’m proud of.”

“So tell me the truth, Aaron, why are you here?”

“I’m still trying to figure that out. Don’t . . . don’t take this the wrong way, but if I passed you on the street I probably wouldn’t look twice. But when you dance, you can stop birds in flight . . . and I guess I’m one of ’em.”

Ava bows her head and chuckles. “I suppose that was a compliment. Thank you.”

“Sorry, I’m really nervous.” Aaron retrieves a handkerchief from an inside coat pocket and mops his expansive forehead.

“Why should you be nervous? You’re not the one dancing.”

“You’re right, you’re right.” The silence builds to an agonizing level. “So . . . so maybe you should start.”

Ava nods and moves to her laptop and cues the audio file. A sweet melody pours from the speakers. She closes her eyes and dances—nothing fancy at first, but as the music progresses, her movements become more fluid. Aaron notices that she doesn’t open her eyes at all, as if seeing the reality of her apartment and him will destroy the art. And the way she holds her imaginary partner makes him wonder what it would feel like to be with her, gliding across the polished floor.

She waltzes for almost an hour, never flagging or taking an awkward step, then sits abruptly on the sofa next to him, not speaking. They finish the bottle of wine, still silent, still wrapped up in the magic of the dance.

The silence again becomes awkward, painful. Finally, Aaron stands and struggles to find his voice. “Can . . . can I come again next Tuesday? I promise just to sit and be quiet.”

She glances sideways at him and frowns. “Well, yes, you may. But I expect you to be more social. You know, talk with me!”

“I’m sorry, I’m out of practice. Where I work, I’m in the paint booth most days and wear a mask. Not much talking going on.”

“See, that’s what I mean. Tell me something about yourself and . . . and I’ll do the same.”

Aaron grins. “I can do that. It’s a deal.”

Every Tuesday night Ava stares out her window at Aaron’s apartment, waiting for the lights to go off, a sure signal that he’s on his way. This Tuesday she is not disappointed. He arrives with the wine. They drink and talk, disclosing each week some tantalizing piece of their lives—he’s a Vietnam War veteran having served with the Airborne, she’s an expert at setting up offshore accounts for her firm’s somewhat-shady clients. Beyond biographical facts, Ava’s and Aaron’s strong emotions slowly color their conversations, exposing their disappointments, months of depression, of anger and resentment, of feeling lost, of feeling found, and of happiness with their growing friendship.

This night, Ava notices that Aaron is more nervous than normal.

“Can I ask you something?” he says after taking a huge gulp of wine.

“Yes, I suppose.”

“Will you teach me to waltz . . . with you?”

She had sensed that he wanted to dance with her but has waited for him to ask, the man’s prerogative, so she’s been told.

“Yes.”

“But look, I’ve been watching you all this time and I’ve looked at online demonstration videos. I’ve practiced a little by myself.”

Ava grins. “I don’t know much about dancing with a partner. So I’ll be a bit clumsy . . . too.”

They both empty their wine glasses. Ava cues the music and they tentatively grasp each other, his hands already wet and shaking. His whole body trembles or maybe part of it is from her. They move slowly. He stares down at his feet. She waits tensely for the first crunch of his heavy shoes on an arthritic foot, vowing not to make a sound. She’s surprised when it doesn’t happen. She keeps her eyes open and stares at his glistening face as he concentrates.

At first, dancing with Aaron feels like being moved around the room by a refrigerator. But as the weeks and months pass, she relaxes and ever so slowly Aaron becomes one of those adroit nineteenth-century gentlemen in evening garb, spinning her around a Vienna dance floor to a Strauss waltz. She hardly notices the pain in her knees and now her hips. But she does notice that it’s more thrilling when she keeps her eyes and heart wide open and focused on Aaron.

The touch of his right hand at the center of her back, his warm left hand grasping hers, gently now with tenderness, the spicy fragrance of his bay rum aftershave tickling her nose, the sound of his deep breathing as if in a waking dream, and the soft thud of his shoes on the hardwood floor, all excite her, make her feel, fill her life with the joy of touch, of movement, of music, of dare she admit, love.

Seasons and years pass. They both retire from their jobs yet still see each other only on Tuesday nights, the high point of Ava’s week. One Tuesday night in 2023, Ava sits at her window and stares at the rectangle of golden light that is Aaron’s apartment. Ghostly figures move behind the curtains. She glances at her watch. It’s past the time when Aaron should arrive; he’s never late. She wonders if he’s sick or maybe just sick of dancing with her and doesn’t want to do it anymore. She turns out the lights in her apartment and weeps. She knows it’s something worse.

The next day Ava talks with the Super. Aaron’s relatives have already taken the body away to someplace in White Plains. By the time she finds a phone number and contacts his younger sister, he’s already in the ground. His sister is surprised that her brother had a shiksa girlfriend and knew nothing of their Tuesday nights together.

Ava continues to dance, but only once or twice a week. Her hips are in bad shape, painful, and she uses a cane. The sound of its soft thud on the hardwood floor reminds her of Aaron and his Florsheims, plodding along. She dances now with her eyes wide open and all the lights turned on, but with the memory of a real dance partner to carry her forward.

Slip knot between one year and another. It’s like falling
through water. Today, I watched a vulture circle high

above the river, beak tilted at the sun, winding her way
to the coastline. She moved through clouds stretching

long to the horizon. What will happen tomorrow?
I thought I’d find answers out west, in mountains

or movement, but I only got good at walking
through weather. I thought I’d know the creature

in this body by now: her red hair and moods, the ache
stuffed in her chest, her changing mind. She wants it all

vibrant and green. I thought I’d get lucky again. Instead,
I return to the store for cartons of eggs. I scrape frost

from my car in the morning. I scroll the news online
at night. The dog wants out and I let her. Someday,

years will loop together and I’ll bundle them around me
in December. Someday, I will fall asleep in a meadow

with wind moving wild and steady. Grass stirring
in a dust-blue haze. Until then, take my hand. Walk beside

this river with me. Let’s throw rocks through the surface
and wait for the splash. Let’s stop and stare at the sky,

at her wandering clouds, her black-winged birds moving
as we move: endless and onward, heading to the sea.

#1

The baby bird has fallen from a tree on Hilltop Lane. A wren. Its legs fold under its tiny body, attached but useless. We can save it, you say, and your husband ushers both of you back to the car, driving slowly to the vet, who takes one look at the bird and sadly shakes his head.

#2

The baby bird has fallen from a tree. It’s cheeping as though nothing’s wrong, but the tree is an oak and the nest is far. You scoop the bird up, its heartbeat thrumming rapidly. You bring it home, feed it milk from an eyedropper, splint its legs with Band-Aids, cheer each small step. We did it, your husband tells you, high-fiving.

#3

The baby bird has fallen from a tree. You say, why did God pick this bird to die? It was in the nest with its siblings, minding its own business, waiting for its mother to bring back a worm or whatever wrens eat and decided to stretch its wings. Did it get too close to the edge? Try to fly too soon? Your husband says, nothing will bring Ella back.

#4

The baby bird has fallen from a tree. You don’t notice, at first. You think leaf or discarded wrapper, something small and forgettable. Its legs broken. Its black eyes barely grazing the asphalt. Alive, but seriously injured. Look, you say to your husband, and he does, before you both keep walking.

to use the word oh in poems
no more than five times in my life. I’ve
squandered one in the first stanza here.
Interjections jiggle a bit as they wait.

Certain substitutes—eh, uh, ah—are
heard among the shuffle-tap rhythms
of my dancing or is that sound my slippers
skipping away? Ah, slippers, you lovely

companions, loyal, oblivious,
drenched in soft colors, stained
with droplets of coffee like blooming
forget-me-nots, I want you to listen

in my final hours. I’ll have the soft
harshness of my breath and a few words
left to whisper. It’s been proved that
breaking hearts make quiet noises

only rodents can hear. Maybe
my final utterance will be noticed
by you and a mouse pausing its gnawing,
then slowly starting again.

“I have a new motto: ‘Act first. Questions be damned!’”

I was standing over Brian’s shoulder. “I have an old motto,” I replied. “A fool and his money are soon parted.”

He took a deep breath, moved the cursor to the “send” button, and clicked.

The instant his credit card cleared, his screen refreshed with thumbnail shots of women, headshots, full body shots, demure, provocative, thoughtful, smiling, laughing, on the couch, at the beach, sprawled on a bench in a park, in pants, in shorts, in dresses and skirts, dark-haired, blonde, young, younger, screen after screen of images of women from the Philippines that CupidPinay.com promised were close matches to Brian’s profile and were eager to meet him.

“See!” he said.

Eight months later, Brian’s clutching a bouquet of roses, I’ve cut short a meeting with my lawyer to be his wingman and we’re watching waves of humanity in its several shapes and textures flow through the international arrivals gate at Pearson Airport’s Terminal 3. He’s wearing tan chinos, new, and a white short-sleeved shirt with blue pinstripes. It’s a hot September day, the AC is pumping, I’m wishing I’d brought a jacket and he’s got these half-moons of sweat blossoming under his arms. He’s out two grand for the flight and whatever else he’s sent her to fix her car, or to buy her a new computer, or to repair the damage to her roof from the storm that hit last month. And that’s just what he’s told me.

He’s not made of money. She knows he’s on workers’ comp with a fucked-up back, retraining as a robotics technician, but to her, I guess that’s good enough, because the poor bastard’s in love and she’s opened the tap.

It’s been an hour since the flight landed, and I’m noticing a few short, brownish people bursting through the automatic doors, but that could be the flight from Lima, I tell him. Brian’s bouncing up on his toes every time the doors slide open with that whooshing sound, like air escaping.

He’s lost weight, a good thing. He’s been taking better care of himself since this started. He’s joined me at the gym and I asked my trainer to put him on a program that wouldn’t hurt his back. He’s straightened out his apartment, too, and he’s taking this robotics thing seriously. Did really well on his last co-op placement. I’m kiting credit cards and he expects he’ll finally have a decent job waiting for him.

But I figure that will only deepen his disappointment when he realizes this is business for her until the well runs dry. I’ve tried to tell him, or at least to prepare him, but how do you do that to a best friend who’s cast himself as the lead in his own fantasy?

“Remember when you and Tracy started, how that’s all you’d talk about?” is his answer, which actually makes my point. Just find a woman you hate and buy her a house. But he’s too smitten to make the connection and I’m putting my lawyer’s kids through college and don’t want to talk about it.

The doors whoosh open and he’s on his toes again. There’s a shriek from somewhere behind us, off to the side an arm waves, people come together, clinging, cheeks moist, and then that big gap-toothed smile thins. He’s flat on his feet once more and he looks over at me, then checks his phone. The flowers still look fresh. He clutches them to his chest, and I imagine the thorns biting through the cloth, but he seems immune to their sting.

I look up at the board. “Lots of international flights landed at the same time,” I say. “They’ll be swamped at Customs and Immigration,” and then there’s an announcement over the PA about a new arrival, Athens, and the crowd stirs and another throng presses in. I look around me. More flowers. Balloons. I should have brought something. I’ll take them to dinner.

The doors slide open and Brian’s back on his toes. He seems to hang there for a moment, and then his lips part and his eyes widen. My hand finds his back. It pushes him forward and I step with him, warmed by the crowd. Kim is plumper than in the photos Brian’s shown me, a bit older, it seems, but the camera flatters, a little round dumpling of a woman, black hair cut shorter than I recall. She scans the crowd. “Brayan,” she calls, and then there’s an instant of recognition when he breaks through. She smiles, big, broad, disarming, and true, and when he thrusts the roses forward, I reach out too. I’m standing at his side as she drops the handle of her suitcase, cries his name once more and rushes toward us.

I did not save it.
That’s the first truth.

It stood in the road
with one wing folded wrong,
black lacquer split along the bone.

It watched me
with an eye that knows I,
that understands traffic,
that has learned what human means.

It slowed.
I could have reached.
The space between us
was not large.

But the crow did not beg.

It did not scatter.

It did not challenge itself
to flee.

It held its ground
like something that already decided.

I thought of hands.

Of lifting.

The way angels do
in stories stiff in hide and faith.

The car behind me inhaled.

The road argued with the brake.

The day kept going.

So I stayed.

Behind the car,
feathers lifted,
no shadow, no cry,
no sudden absolution.

Only later did I feel it:
the weight of having chosen
nothing remarkable.

Crows remember faces.

They carry debts.

They gather in mourning.

If it calls me back,
I will not pretend I know it not.

I knew
what I was doing
when I kept my feet
still to the road.

Eleanor lay awake beside her husband thinking, I wouldn’t mind if his genitals fell off, leaving behind the smooth bump of a pelvis, and I never had sex again. She’d borne Franklin six children and eulogized one; subsequently sex seemed a duty long overachieved.

Eleanor instead thought edaciously of Hick, of taking the woman in her arms and holding. These were not thoughts meant for a first lady, but thoughts for when the world was settled and sleeping, and Eleanor was only a woman. Then, Eleanor stopped holding her breath and let truth fill the empty spaces in her lungs.

after Art & Remembrance by Esther Nisenthal Krinitz (1927–2001)
at the American Visionary Art Museum, Baltimore, Maryland

In this gallery, Mother, your memory lingers along
with your Noah’s Ark embroidery kit framed for my

childhood wall now hanging in my office all these decades
later. Your playful pairs of animals parading down a garden

path and you laughed away its artistry—I just filled in
the lines. How you would have revered this woman’s

embroidered atlas of survival in a life your emigrant parents
escaped just in time. Esther’s threads bear the needle’s prayer

fired through the eyes of woman’s art of fiber. What is a text
before it’s a text? Her hands, pollinators taking bits from

here and there to make something new, story cloths for
the one stitch at a time, each trembling to call on memory.

Threads pulled in, then out, to embed the shudder and spar
of moments lived. Mniszek, her shtetl, idyllic in simplicity.

Yes, those are the horses and wagons and thatched roofs
and the love of soil with chickens and geese everywhere.

This is a story of loops, faith in the telling; bravery of tender
pigtails whose childhood vanished when the black-on-black

clouds entered and the war invaded. Jewish boys digging tank
trenches, shot in the woods, her roll calls of neighbors in wagons

bound for death camps, as she and her sister hid in fields and
forests or masqueraded in other villages as Catholic farm girls.

After liberation she ached for signs of what happened to her family.
At Maidanek she found piles of dust-covered shoes and rows of

giant cabbages thriving in fields made rich with human ashes.
In her final panel, June 10, 1949, the Statue of Liberty reaches

above her new family with a chorus of sea gulls circling. What lives
outside that freeze-framed sky we call hope, is a reminder through the

politics in textile—for today’s Mother of Exiles stands weary as the
hinges of her golden doors corrode in the squalls of intoxicated power.

I suppose no one would accuse me of indifference. He was a stray dog. People passed through the nearby residential blocks every day; I was not the only one who saw him. None of them stopped to help him. At least I fed him.

After I first saw him, I began to bring him food every day. That afternoon, I had just finished grocery shopping at Aeon and was riding my electric scooter home when I saw him on a small path near my neighborhood. He was a black dog. I don’t know why I stopped. Maybe it was the wounds covering his body. Big and small, some still wet with blood, some already scabbed over. Probably bites from other dogs. Or his eyes. His tail tucked, something in his gaze I couldn’t name. Looking at him, I was reminded of the dogs I had seen as a child outside a dog meat shop, in cages by the entrance. They had that same look in their eyes. My chest tightened. Or maybe he reminded me of the dog I had when I was ten. When we moved to the town, my parents gave her to our neighbors. When I left, she tried to follow me, but the chain around her neck held her back. She stood there, looking at me, whimpering. I walked away. She was still looking at me. I still think of her sometimes. That chain, less than a meter long. She never ran across the grass again. Never lay on her back at my feet, waiting for me to rub her belly. Her world became that small yard. She walked slowly inside it, like an old person with a cane, each step careful, one after another.

For eight days in a row, every evening, I brought a bag of dog food, a bottle of water, and two bowls to that path. At first he hid in the grass, watching me from a distance. I poured the food into one bowl and water into the other. Then I crossed to the other side of the path and stood under a tree, far from him. I smiled at him. He looked at me, then at the bowls. People say animals can sense kindness. I walked away slowly. When I turned back, he was already devouring the food. It was late October. The mornings and evenings were cold. I should have prepared a cardboard box for him, or at least left him some old clothes.

You don’t see many stray dogs in Guangzhou. They say it’s because the public security bureau organizes teams to patrol the streets and capture and relocate them. The nearest holding facility was less than an hour’s drive from my home. I could have called the police, asked them to take him in. Maybe that would have eased my conscience.

But it was already too late. I told myself someone must have taken him away. That he had been hurt.

I shouldn’t have hesitated. I kept wondering whether I should take him home. On the third day, he dared to come closer to me. On the fourth, he wagged his tail and let me touch his head. Even after everything the world had done to him, he still trusted people. He would have been a gentle, obedient dog. He would have known how to cherish a home. If I had taken him in, he would have been my most loyal companion. I wouldn’t have had to come back every day to an empty apartment. He would have been there when I returned from work, sat with me while I ate, walked with me in the evenings, slept beside me at night. We could have been happy together.

I should have decided sooner. If I had acted at once, if I hadn’t let him down, he would be here now, tongue out, grinning at me. But he disappeared. Next to the bowls, there was only a darkened patch of blood. I heard the security guards had driven him away with sticks. I heard someone had complained. I heard they were afraid he might have rabies. He waited on that path every day for me to come back. He knew I would. He thought I cared about him. He thought we would become a family.

I remember a romp
to the village store.

The shelves were tall
and packed with candy.

My brother thought that
stuff was free,

and filled his pockets
shamelessly.

I knew we had
no money.

The aproned ogre
called the cops

who asked our names
and where we lived.

Mum stood in curlers
holding a mop

when the cruiser pulled up
by the kitchen door.

I must have been five,
and my brother just four

when we first rode with cops
and played robbers.

Yesterday, the neon goddess arrived, running from the law with a broken jaw and a fistful of promissory notes she claimed were redeemable, but were not.

Never saw that in the cards. And I look twice a day.

I made her a milkshake and let her sack out on the couch. She spoke in whispers through the wires on her face. I had to lean in close to hear her. When I did, my hair became entangled in her apparatus. “You’re too bright,” I said. “You’ll blind me.”

But the truth is, she had already blinded and entangled me years before.

We were inseparable. Neon and Jade. We cut classes together. We hung out in BART stations, begging for change and snatching purses. She would cause a diversion and I’d grab and run. Playing to type. I was the fast one. She was the drama queen.

It worked great until we started dropping it all on drugs.

This was the nineties. Ancient history. But we’re both still scamming, each in our own way. I draw astrological charts, cast the I Ching, and see the future in the tarot. But only an idiot would ask my advice. I can’t even figure out my own life.

And Neon? She’s selling on the street. I didn’t ask how that was working out, but she told me anyway.

“Prison’s a royal bitch. Half my lights have gone out.”

“You still shine bright to me,” I told her, my eyes stinging. “Bright as ever.”

pieces.html:
Everything is reversible, says a man
who has never counted out 24 weeks
on the left-most 7 knuckles of his hand just to keep track of how
many days lying by omission would work
before everyone with eyes becomes an accomplice
or a runaway car. I’m happy
with my delightful birth-defected deaf cat screaming at me
to wake up and smell the vomit he so kindly deposited
beneath the roses. I’m happy
with my cousin in tears stringing along the phone line. I’m happy
with “babygirl” being flexible as long as it’s warm. I’m happy
with prenups and European passports. I’m happy with all that
is reversible, which yeah sure, is most things, but baby,
nothing ever really gets taken back. We just forget
to be happy with what we have. I do it too, I don’t want to
do it to us. Want to stop seeing
what I do: a hidden shine
on the unrippled lake surface insisting
on itself, whispering in circles that
I saw it in the mirror over my shoulder
back when only my Barbies were getting divorced.
They were always walking out of Roman stone court buildings
with their plastic heads taped on
loose. They were bad bitches, bad daughters, bad wives,
and yet they stepped across the inch-high threshold of their homes
and let me click their briefcases open knowing I was hoping
for ten million dollars or a human embryo
gazing up at me like a stillborn lamb.
I always pictured it half-dead so
I could nurse it back
to my life. Never could believe the universe would give me anything
I could easily share. Always knew I’d have to work for it, knew that
I wouldn’t be the only one bleeding when they cut
the cord away forever
only half symbolically.
