The ship came down over Ban Sai Yai during badminton, which everybody agreed afterwards was unfortunate, because Dao had been winning for the first time in her life and now nobody would ever be able to confirm it.

It had the general shape of a cathedral that had swallowed a second cathedral and was thinking about a third. It lowered itself onto the school field with tremendous care and flattened the net. The net belonged to the district office, which meant forms.

Khru Ampai stood at her gate with her stick in one hand and a bag of limes in the other. She had taught at that school for most of her life and had assessed many arriving vehicles from this exact spot, and she had learned that you could tell a great deal from the parking. This one had the sort of confidence that came from having never been asked to park anywhere else.

“Waan,” she said. “Come and look.”

Her wife came out of the kitchen, drying her hands on her apron, and looked for a while.

“They’ve flattened the net.”

Waan looked at the ship. “That seems excessive.”

A ramp descended from the underside and stopped at a height that implied somebody, somewhere, had been asked how tall the people of Ban Sai Yai were. Down it came in a complicated arrangement of limbs, joints, and formal-looking folds, as though its skeleton had been designed by a committee that had never met a skeleton. It also had too many elbows.

It arranged itself at the bottom of the ramp, unfolded a document that continued unfolding for longer than the ramp could support, and addressed the school field.

“I am Hessenwaal Pree, Latter Voice of the Perpetual Amity of Thurn, Ambassador Extraordinary and Without Foreseeable End, Keeper of the Grievance,” it said. “I am here about the ladder.”

The children said nothing. Dao picked up her racquet.

“I will require your Disinterested Party.”

“Our what?” said Waan.

“Whoever lives nearest the object,” said Pree. “The Book of Settled Practice is specific.”

Every head on the field turned towards the gate, and within seconds Ampai had somehow become the nearest authority on extraterrestrial parking.

The Book of Settled Practice arrived at the district office that evening in a crate. Fon signed for it, because Fon signed for everything, and then she read it, because she had discovered that if you left paperwork unattended, it developed ambitions.

Fon had been in Ampai’s class years ago and was the only child who ever read the whole textbook, including the appendix, including the publisher’s address. She worked in records now. She arrived at the house before sunrise with the crate roped to the back of her motorbike and the relevant sections marked with torn strips of till receipt.

“It is a legal code,” Fon said. “It governs every settled civilisation. There are twelve thousand and eleven clauses. Four of them are about biscuits.”

“Sit down,” said Ampai. “Waan, tea.”

“I would rather stand while I explain it.”

“Then stand.”

Fon stood. “Two powers are at war. The Perpetual Amity of Thurn and the Gracious Reciprocity of Klaad.”

“Those are both friendly names.”

“Yes. They are at war. The Book of Settled Practice says a grievance concerning a borrowed object must be arbitrated at the object’s last recorded location, by the person living nearest to it, in a venue of no strategic value whatsoever.”

Waan put down the tea. “The hall.”

“The multipurpose hall behind the temple,” Fon agreed. “I checked. It has no strategic value whatsoever.”

The hall had been assessed for strategic value twice. The first assessment found none. The second confirmed it. There had not been a third, because nobody had wanted to interfere with the result.

Ampai turned a lime over in her fingers. “And the object is here.”

“The object has been here a very long time,” said Fon. “They have been fighting over it, and nobody thought to come and look.”

They set up the hall the way they did for funerals and vaccination day, which is to say plastic chairs in rows and the good fan brought down from the head monk’s room. Ampai had the whiteboard wheeled in. The marker only worked if you held it at an angle, and Ampai had done so for years, which was long enough for the district to consider the problem solved.

The Thurn delegation entered first and unfolded into the left-hand chairs. The Klaad delegation came in through the other door and had to be helped, because Vuun of the Sorrows was wide enough to make the plastic chairs look optimistic, and in the end she settled onto the floor with her attendants arranged around her, and became, for the remainder of the week, a very expensive sofa with opinions.

“I will not sit opposite that,” said Vuun.

“Then sit at an angle,” said Ampai.

“Do you have any idea what that creature’s grandmother did?”

“I have not met your grandmother either. Sit at an angle.”

Vuun sat at an angle.

Ampai went to the whiteboard and wrote two words in her enormous teacher’s hand. PREE. VUUN.

“That is you,” she said. “I am not saying the rest. If I say the rest, we will be here until the mangoes come in.”

Pree drew itself up through several of its elbows. “My title is a record of service.”

“Your title is a record of a person with nothing else to fill the morning. Hands up before you speak. Nobody speaks over anybody. If you speak over somebody, I will write your name in the corner.”

“In the corner,” Pree repeated.

“Yes.”

“Is that considered a sanction?”

“No. It is the corner.”

Pree looked at the corner again.

There was a long pause. Out on the field, Dao and her brother were putting the badminton net back up, using the wreckage of the old posts and a length of blue nylon rope, and the sound of that carried in through the shutters.

Pree looked at the whiteboard. Vuun looked at the whiteboard. Neither of them had been given an instruction by a person smaller than a building in living memory, and the sensation was so novel that both of them wanted to see where it went.

Vuun raised what she used instead of a hand.

“Yes.”

“May I say what they did to the ladder?”

“You may.”

The grievance took most of the morning. Pree read every word, including the parts written by lawyers whose entire civilisation had since been folded into another civilisation and lost, because the wording was still the wording.

The facts were these. A long time ago, longer ago than either side could now pronounce with confidence, the Perpetual Amity of Thurn had lent the Gracious Reciprocity of Klaad a ladder.

“A ladder,” said Ampai.

“A ladder,” said Pree.

“Go on.”

The ladder came back. That much was agreed. Klaad had returned it, and Thurn had received it, and there the trouble started, because it arrived with paint on it, and a rung missing, but most of all, it arrived without thanks.

“Paint,” said Ampai, writing it on the board.

“Paint,” said Pree.

“What colour?”

Pree consulted the document. Pree consulted several attendants. The attendants consulted one another in a language of filing cabinets going downhill.

“The record does not say.”

“Write it down, Fon. Colour not recorded.” Ampai capped the marker. “Next.”

Next was the schedule of previous attempts to settle the matter. One had ended over the seating. One had ended over the seating at the one before. One had ended because the Klaad delegation arrived in the correct number of vehicles and Thurn assumed the number was intended to make a point.

“How many have there been?” said Ampai.

“This is the twelfth,” said Pree.

“And what happened at the eleventh?”

Pree checked. “The eleventh is what the tenth was about.”

Vuun’s answer took the afternoon. Klaad had never painted the ladder. Klaad had lent it onward, which Klaad was entitled to do, and it had gone out across half the Reciprocity and been used for orchards and for roofing and for one celebrated rescue at the flood locks, and had come home with the ordinary marks of an object that has been used.

“Then the paint belongs to somebody else,” said Ampai.

“The paint is history,” said Vuun.

“Whose?”

“An orchard’s. They had it at a wedding. It came back with rice on it as well, and we took the rice off. That is recorded as an improvement.”

“An improvement.”

“The only one in the schedule.”

“The paint must belong to somebody else, and you’ve just forgotten to clean it off.” Ampai put a small tick next to PAINT.

“That is not the same as breaking it. Pree, is it the same as breaking it?” Ampai said.

Pree was silent for a while. “No.”

“Say it towards her, not towards me.”

“No,” said Pree, at an angle.

By mid-week the whiteboard said PAINT and RUNG and NO THANKS, and under that, in smaller letters, because Fon had asked for it, the note that the war had run long enough for both sides to forget which of them built the ladder, and that they were now fighting about the document recording who had forgotten.

There was also the question of whether something lent onward remained, in law, lent, which occupied an entire session and produced more heat than the fan could move.

“Lending is a chain,” said Vuun. “Each link holds.”

“Lending is a chain,” Pree agreed, “and you handed our link to a stranger.”

“Because it was useful. A ladder in a vault is a plank with ambitions.”

“Our vault has a plaque,” said Pree. “The plaque is longer than the ladder. There was a ceremony. I was not born, and I have seen the footage, and it is difficult to sit through. The applause lasts eleven minutes.”

“Hands,” said Ampai.

Both of them put up a hand.

“Fon. What does the book say?”

Fon turned to her strip of till receipt. “Clause nine hundred and forty. A thing lent may be lent onward where the onward use is consistent with the thing’s nature.”

“And the nature of a ladder,” said Ampai, “is going up.”

“The clause does not specify.”

“Then I am specifying. Write it down.”

Pree’s hand went up again.

“Yes.”

“If they used the ladder for going up, as a ladder is for going up, then our complaint is the paint, and you have already established that the paint does not constitute a grievance.”

“Yes.”

“I have travelled a considerable distance to establish that the paint does not constitute a grievance.”

“Yes,” said Ampai. “Sit down. Your name is not in the corner. That is the best I can do on a Wednesday.”

Outside, the ship had been asked to move a short distance to the left, because the school field was needed, and to everyone’s astonishment it had. The children were selling iced drinks to the attendants through the fire door at a price that rose across the week and that nobody in the Gracious Reciprocity of Klaad thought to query.

By then the attendants had discovered the morning market. They went through it in a line, stooping under the awnings, buying things they had no use for, and the market let them, because they paid without haggling and were pleasant about the dogs, cats, grasshoppers, and snakes. Dao’s grandmother taught one of them to fold a banana leaf. It carried the leaf home and showed it to the Reciprocity. The Reciprocity was not interested, so it showed them again.

At the point in the proceedings when Waan brought in the food, the Office of Ratification arrived.

He came through the fire door, which was propped open with a breeze block, a small grey creature with a stamp on a lanyard. His name was Bib, and he was the happiest creature any of them had ever hosted.

“I am terribly sorry,” said Bib, radiating delight. “This is void.”

“On what grounds?” said Fon.

“On the grounds that the Disinterested Party is required to be disinterested, and she is not, because she has been provided with lunch.”

Ampai looked at the trays. Sticky rice in baskets. Waan’s nam phrik, the one with the burnt shallots, in the cracked blue bowl she refused to throw out. Fried river fish, still going.

“Lunch,” said Bib, “constitutes a benefit.”

“Sit down, Bib,” said Ampai.

“I am afraid I really cannot. Once I have said void, it is void. I have a stamp.”

Fon took another strip of till receipt from the crate and turned to the page it marked. She didn’t look up while she read. The page was staying put, and there was no need to give it the satisfaction of making her follow it with her eyes.

“Clause four thousand and nine,” she said. “Where refreshment has been offered and accepted in the presence of both parties, the parties are held to have entered into hospitality. Hospitality binds. A binding may not be voided by an officer who has also eaten.”

Everybody turned to Bib. A piece of fried river fish was halfway to what passed for his face.

“That is a very old clause.”

“It is clause four thousand and nine,” said Fon. “Just before the biscuits.”

“I have only had a little. I thought it would be rude not to finish it.”

“Sit down, Bib,” said Ampai, and Bib sat down, and Waan gave him another piece, and he took it, and after that Bib was on nobody’s side at all and enjoyed the rest of the week more than any of them.

Vuun ate the nam phrik out of politeness and then ate the rest of it for reasons that became increasingly difficult to explain, then asked, through an attendant, whether the shallots were burnt on purpose. Waan said yes. Vuun went quiet in the manner of a civilisation revising its position on several things at once.

They found the ladder because Fon went and stood in the temple courtyard and looked up, which was the one thing nobody in the galaxy had done.

It was lashed to the wall of the bell tower under the eaves, out of the rain, where it had been kept for as long as anybody could remember. Bringing it down took four men, and the head monk’s instructions, which were unhelpful, and he admitted as much afterwards.

They carried it into the hall and laid it on the tables, and the Perpetual Amity of Thurn and the Gracious Reciprocity of Klaad stood over the thing they had been killing one another over, and looked at it.

It was a ladder. It had paint on it.

It had a great deal of paint on it. It had the red from the Songkran festival two head monks ago, and under that the flaking cream from when the school was cream, and a run of gold leaf on the top rung where somebody had been careless with the Buddha’s shoulder and had put a hand out on the way down.

Pree set a manipulator against the split end where the layers showed and counted them back, one civilisation of paint at a time. It reached the cream and stopped. The stiles were worn pale and smooth in the two places where hands go. One rung was new mango wood. The one below it was teak out of Somsak’s bed frame. The one below that carried a bracket of galvanised strap around the joint, because Ampai’s grandfather had opened his palm on the split and had fixed it because nobody else would.

Every lantern festival, the ladder went up the bell tower with rope and came down with something else fixed, until nobody could remember which parts belonged to the original ladder.

“There is a rung missing,” said Pree.

“There is not,” said Ampai.

“The record says a rung is missing.”

“The record is old. We put it back.” She laid her stick against the mango wood, pale and clean and with another life left in it. “We have put it back many times. That is what a rung is for.”

Vuun had moved without anyone catching her moving, which at that size was an achievement, and had one manipulator resting on the smooth place in the stile where the hands go.

“This is worn,” said Vuun.

“Yes,” said Ampai.

“Is it worn because it was used?”

“Yes,” said Ampai.

“We kept it in a case,” said Vuun.

“We kept it in a vault,” said Pree, “with the case.”

They looked at each other across the table, two powers with enough ordnance between them to unmake a spiral arm, who each had spent an unimaginable span of their history guarding a photograph of a ladder.

Ampai let the silence sit. She had been teaching long enough to know that silence had a useful life, and that if you gave it another few seconds it became somebody else’s problem.

Then she said, “The paint is settled. The rung is settled. Neither of you crossed the sky for a splotch of paint.”

Pree’s elbows folded down, one after another, until Pree was nearer the table than the ceiling.

“They did not thank us.”

“No,” said Ampai.

“We lent it,” said Pree. “It went all across the Reciprocity. It was in the orchards. It was at the flood locks when the children were on the roof. Everybody sang about the flood locks afterwards. There are twelve songs about the flood locks. There is a monument. There is a public holiday. Nobody has ever once said, ‘That was your ladder.’”

Vuun was silent for a while. The fan turned. Outside, Dao’s brother was practising the festival drum and tangling the second bar, the way he always did.

“It had no name on it when it reached us,” Vuun said. “By then it had been ours so long. We thought it had always been there.”

“Now say the part you’ve left out,” said Ampai.

Vuun’s attendants shifted.

“Say it towards her.”

“We had your ladder,” said Vuun. “We used it for years and failed to mention it. This was poor administration. Thank you.”

Pree folded its elbows and pushed the document off the table. It landed in the dust beside the breeze block and the flattened remains of the district’s badminton net, where it looked no more important than anything else in the hall.

Bib stamped the grievance, the breeze block, and the net, and beamed.

Then Fon raised another difficulty. By then everyone had learned that if a difficulty existed, Fon would find it.

“Whose is it now?”

“Mine,” said Ampai.

“You cannot say mine, Khru. The Book of Settled Practice requires a determination,” said Fon.

“Then determine this.” Ampai put her hand flat on the top rung, on the gold leaf, where the Buddha’s shoulder had come away on somebody’s careless thumb. “It has my grandfather’s strap on it and Somsak’s bed frame in it and paint off every building in this village. If it was ever theirs, it isn’t any more. We mended it, and a thing that has been mended enough belongs to whoever did the mending.”

“That is not in the Book of Settled Practice,” said Fon.

“Write it in. There is room. There are twelve thousand clauses and four of them are about biscuits,” said Ampai.

“Then it is yours,” said Vuun. “We have crossed half the known civilisations for a ladder that now belongs to a schoolteacher.”

“No,” said Ampai. “You have come a very long way to borrow a ladder. You may as well do it properly.”

The hall went quiet.

“Lantern festival is in the dry season. The rope goes up the bell tower, and the ladder needs one person at the bottom and one at the top. Last year I did both, which is not a sensible arrangement.”

She took her hand off the top rung.

“So you will come. Both of you. One at the bottom and one at the top. You have spent the week deciding whose ladder it is. You can spend one day putting it to work.”

“And then it is ours,” said Pree.

“And then you bring it back,” said Ampai. “That is the point of a ladder. You do not keep a ladder. A ladder is for lending.”

Vuun made a sound her attendants afterwards refused to translate.

“Write the date on the board, Fon. They will want it in writing. They are that sort.”

Fon wrote the date. Both delegations photographed the board. Fon wrote down that they had photographed it. One of the delegations photographed that.

The Perpetual Amity of Thurn and the Gracious Reciprocity of Klaad have returned every dry season since. Pree goes up, because Pree unfolds, and Vuun holds the bottom, because Vuun is not going anywhere. They bring the rope. They are permitted to bring nothing else, on Waan’s instruction, except for the year they brought a case of something from the Reciprocity that had been banned there for three hundred years and was now apparently very good with rice. The head monk laughed until he had to sit down. After that, they were permitted to bring that as well.

Dao beat her brother on the school field that first dry season with the whole of the Gracious Reciprocity of Klaad watching from the touchline. There were witnesses. It is recorded at the district office, and Fon has the paper.

The war is over. The Book of Settled Practice records the reason for its ending in a new clause, near the end, after the biscuits, in language that took a committee an entire session to agree, and which Fon, who holds the only copy on this planet and keeps it in the records office under a fan, has translated as follows.

A ladder belongs to whoever has repaired it often enough to know which rung will fail next. A ladder kept in a case belongs to nobody, and the case is not evidence. If you lend a ladder, remember that somebody else will use it. If you borrow a ladder, return the ladder. If it comes back in better condition than you lent it, say thank you.

Underneath, in the section reserved for places of no strategic value whatsoever, there is now an entry for Ban Sai Yai, and the entry says only that this is where the ladder is.

The badminton net has been replaced. There were lots of forms.

pieces.html:
“Nothing”
is a failure in observation
brought on, at times,
by the deflated hopes
of the eager in waiting

as if the honey-colored tea
filling the glass cup
on the oaken surface of a table
were to suddenly take the stage
and explain
its bright and gory origins,

of how it was plucked,
green-leafed and oblivious
from under a glowing sun,
then rootless, might have wished
to wander, but instead withered,
shoulder-to-shoulder
with the most aromatic
but unintelligible of companions.

I will spare you
the parts about chopping, darkness,
damp pungency, so you, too,
will brighten when you remember
again the cup, the honey-colored tea
when you say nothing.

My father spent years moving us everywhere but back to where he came from, avoiding the north of England as though it might snatch him back if he got too close. But the north of England came everywhere with us. His Now Then instead of Hello, his cheddar cheese on fruitcake, his quiet queerness, the belly, the jokes.

This week he gets lost in the car park at his favourite restaurant. The waiters come out to help their big spender—into the chair, into the tasting menu. The owner brings a brandy and says, my friend, we told you to get well before driving again. You can tell a Yorkshireman, my father says, but you can’t tell him much.

At the hospital they treat the head wound. His brothers descend from the north to his bedside. The morphine works (What’s the difference between a buffalo and a bison? You can’t wash your hands in a—); the nurse tweezes glass into a dish, my father asks her to the youth dance at the social club. The brothers are thin and grey. They can’t find the punchlines.

pieces.title: My Heart is a Bird
pieces.author: Bull Garlington
pieces.html: My heart is a bird I caught by accident. A starling flew into my hand. I tried to let it go but it only flapped into my chest, where it preened and chirped its space laser song. I left the door open (it can leave anytime it wants) but instead of escaping it tells me all day long how much it loves me; it cheeps and chitters you are incredible over and over, its warbling code (dot dash, dot dash) so simple to decipher: please and thank you, call and response, shrink or grow bigger, seek or withdraw. For months and months, it’s fluttered and flitted and in this time I’ve learned a little about ornithology. First, that it’s not a starling—not only a starling: it’s a flock of pigeons, ratty and dumb; it’s a seaside gull, witless and greedy; it’s an Alabama silkie screaming into the rising sun; it’s a peregrine falcon falling silently from its perch on the forty-fifth floor of the Willis Tower not to hunt, not to kill, but for the joy it feels in the geometry of its flight and always, always, always my bird is ready, my bird watches, feathered head cocked, listening, having heard tell, having caught sight, having felt through the wide-open mesh of my spirit, my paper-thin and ancient skin, the sudden crunch of gravel on a driveway that leads to a fire, some new beauty, a gleaming Buick Skylark rolling slowly into a dry wicket, a word, a note, a glance that carries in its minuscule body a world of truth and a spark of love and my bird beats a wing and my bird lifts its head and my bird, my phoenix bursts into cinnamon and tangerine my face a murmuration of tears and my heart catches in its cage, wings beating faster to pump a salty truth: that I’m not a cage, I’m a chariot, a pagan parade float, a temple for the simplest fact, that love is everywhere and I get some and I give some and my heart, my feathered heart, is a bird.

pieces.html:
Amalia befriended the crows by accident. When her husband, César, “took a job,” as he said, in another state and slowly stopped calling her on Sundays after Mass, she took it as quiet permission to do all the projects he’d disallowed during their twenty-seven years of marriage. In her first act of aloneness, she painted the dry shutters of their stumpy, brown house the juicy pink of ripe prickly pears. Sanding the splintery shutters in preparation was just as unpleasant as César had predicted many years ago when she’d first suggested repainting, but when she smoothed the first stroke of hot pink against the soft wood, she felt the movement vibrate down her arm and into her chest, as if a musical string had been plucked within her body. Feeling like a divine instrument, she painted every shutter in careful layers, and then the front door, too. The neighbors called the color “loud.” Amalia called it perfect.

Next, she bought tiny, brittlebush-yellow chicks from the local feed store and put them in the long-empty coop that came with the house. The chicks brought fresh life to her dusty yard, peeping and scratching at the dirt with comical determination, like children playing at being adults. They grew with astonishing quickness, transitioning from puffballs that huddled under the heat lamp to awkward, long-legged birds that pecked at each other when food ran low. Amalia became concerned when several started emitting patchy, long squawks that were clearly a teenage version of rooster crows. Ay, she thought, the neighbors will complain.

Amalia did not mention the success of her bright shutters and her growing chicks to César when he called; she’d never been one to say, “I told you so.” But, she felt emboldened enough to start an open compost pile for her garden trimmings (minimal) and food waste (maximal), much to the satisfaction of the local skunks. The compost pile, which César had adamantly refused to sanction for decades due to a fear of attracting rats and making their sparse, flat yard look “trashy,” also perturbed Amalia’s neighbors.

She could admit that the skunks were not an ideal addition to Ocatillo Street, though she liked the way they pranced across her yard, carrying their dainty tails aloft like parasols. And, while their stench sometimes hung so greasy in the air that she could taste it, their obvious enjoyment of her compost pile felt like a private kudos, a pat on the back that she would never get from César. So, Amalia was almost reluctant to see the skunks abandon her yard when the crows asserted dominance over the wilted cabbage, coffee grounds, slimy cilantro, dried petunias, and the rest of the mixed organic detritus that her new, single life created in a pile in the southeast corner of the yard.

Once the crows discovered the heap, they claimed it expediently and with no mercy, diving fearlessly at the skunks like black harpoons from the sky. The skunks proved cowardly against the noisy birds, loping away rather than standing their ground. Adiós, skunks, Amalia thought, as she watched the last one wiggle under her fence and trot off into the desert sunset like some lily-livered bandit from an old, black-and-white western.

“Hasta la vista, Stinky,” she muttered, and then shook her head at her own silliness. She pictured César’s incredulous face whenever he caught her talking to herself, and she felt instantly self-conscious, her hands squeezing the dishtowel tightly, creating cream-colored lines in the folds of her wide knuckles. Sighing deeply, she carefully relaxed her fingers, slung the dishtowel over her shoulder, and gazed slowly around her living room, verifying that she was alone and free to mutter. Up on the power lines that ran in front of her house, two crows cawed victoriously.

At first, the prevalence of the crows in Amalia’s yard made her a bit uneasy. Her great-aunt always said that the hoot of an owl foretold death and the caw of a crow served as a warning, but as a child, Amalia could never understand what the warnings meant. When she heard the crows cawing in the palo verde tree that bloomed in Títi Marta’s front yard, Amalia knew she had been warned, but had no inkling of why. What was she supposed to do differently? What was the message? The crows of her childhood were unsettling and unclear, and these days Amalia wasn’t in any mood for spooky messages; she was a grown woman with no time for all that nonsense.

The crows acted guarded around her, too, always keeping an eye on her if she went outside to fetch the mail, to add to the compost pile, to water the droopy marigolds in their cracked pots on her front steps. Her presence made the crows scatter nervously, feathers fluttering, cawing loudly to one another in warning. Their fear pleased her; it felt like respect.

Amalia had an excellent view of the compost pile from the window over her kitchen sink, and she often watched the crows while she did the dishes. One crow would scout the pile, fly away to collect its peers, and return to eat together as a group. The scout crow never gorged himself on the tastiest bits of the pile before fetching the others, which seemed so equitable, so thoughtful. The skunks never did that; it was every skunk for himself in the compost heap. The crows were also much pickier than the skunks, which ate everything. The crows liked grapes, but not citrus; tortillas, but not cantaloupe; eggs, but not fibrous kale stems. Their choosiness felt classy, somehow, as if the compost pile was not a heap of garbage, but rather a collection of treats to be sifted through with care.

One still spring day when the air smelled of sticky creosote, and the dust was mostly staying on the ground, Amalia looked out the window and found that the crows had pulled all the avocado peels out of the compost heap and created their own mini-pile five feet away from the central heap. She went outside, gathered the brown peels, and dropped them into the trash bin. If the crows felt these peels were not worthy of the compost pile, so be it.

A few weeks later, when the creosote was blooming yellow and the beavertail cactus were sprouting pink buds, the crows grew especially loud. She looked up from the book she was reading on the porch and saw them attacking a rat that had clearly been headed for the compost heap. Her first thought was, Thank God César is not here to see that rat. Then her brain slowed as she watched the crows attack as a mob, beaks flashing, swiftly killing the rat before eating it. They swallowed chunks of fresh rat flesh with the cool remorselessness of professional assassins, squawking loudly as they ate. Amalia wondered if their satisfied caws were a warning to any other rats in the area. She hoped so; she found that she liked the idea of her compost being under crow protection.

After a few weeks, Amalia’s initial unease about the crows’ warnings wore off entirely; instead, she looked forward to the sound of their caws approaching as they flew up the street or swooped in from the desert. They were certainly more entertaining than anything on TV, and she often watched them from her porch. The crows seemed to converse the whole time they ate, picking through her discards, discussing the best pieces, and flying away while chatting about the meal they’d just had, leaving a straggler or two behind to guard the pile.

One Sunday, the phone didn’t ring after Mass for her usual check-in with César. Amalia felt surprised to discover that she did not miss him, though when he first left, she had sometimes found the house oddly quiet without his MMA on the TV or his baseball games on the radio, which he insisted was the only way to really appreciate baseball.

“You have to truly listen to follow the game when it’s on the radio; it’s better than TV. Real fans are radio people. Don’t you see, Ami?” he’d asked her too many times. But she didn’t see, and honestly, she didn’t care. She didn’t miss the sound of baseball on the radio, and with the crows in her yard now, there was plenty of noise. None of the new noise was radio ads with stupid jingles designed to sell car parts or antacids for old men; Amalia felt she had upgraded her soundscape significantly.

After months of daily visits from the crows, Amalia started to feel distinctly that they were sometimes cawing at her about the items she added to the compost heap. The lookout crow, whom she had privately named Loupe due to the way he studied her from above with a critical eye, watched her adding yard trimmings, or tamale husks, or carrot tops to the heap. Loupe seemed to comment on each item in a variety of low caws and clicks, and then either fly off to collect his crew or—and this was more and more common—just caw loudly as if reporting the daily menu to his fellow crows within earshot.

Loupe often remained on a high perch while his buddies feasted on the pile; perhaps his job was to ensure their safety. Amalia began saving a few special scraps for him, which she placed in the yard after the departure of the big group—she refused to think of them as a murder. Loupe craned his neck and watched her carefully as she put his meal out, waiting for her to go back to the porch before coming down for his private reward.

The habit she developed of saving Loupe his own meal made Amalia feel like a housewife from the olden days, the kind that didn’t work and wore tailored dresses to vacuum their carpeted homes. Had any such wives ever existed, or had they only been characters on TV when she was little? Amalia was not sure, but she imagined Loupe coming home from a hard day’s work, briefcase under his wing, to find the meal she saved for him still warming in the oven. She didn’t have carpet, and her bosom would never fit in a tight TV-dress, but she chuckled to herself, doubly pleased by the image and her ability to make herself laugh. Then a third wave of satisfaction rolled through her when she realized she could laugh as loud as she wanted, and no one would ask her in an irritated tone, “Hey, what’s so funny?” No one was there demanding to be let in on the joke.

On a particularly dusty Thursday during a particularly dry summer, Amalia went to the feed store for more chicken scratch. Her chickens were producing eggs now. She felt like a homesteader from Little House on the Prairie. So capable, so independent. Plus, every egg offered proof that César had been wrong for all those years when he said, “No, no, no!” to filling their coop.

The chickens had very little personality, especially when compared to the crows. The week prior, Amalia had witnessed one of her Rhode Island Reds trying to fight a reflection of itself in an old mirror leaning against the shed she was cleaning out. The fight lasted for hours; she had to shoo the hen away to make it quit its frenzied self-assault. Amalia decided that she felt no guilt about consuming such an idiotic bird. Better to put you in an enchilada, she thought, as she ushered the tired hen back to the coop.

But the crows were different, smarter than she’d suspected, aggressive but also charming and sly. So when she went to buy chicken scratch, she asked the whiskery shopkeeper at the Blooming Desert Hay & Feed Store what to get for crows. With no judgment on his lined face and not a single word, he added a huge bag of peanuts in their shells to her cart.

At first, Amalia had thrown some peanuts onto the compost pile, but it felt wrong, like dirtying up the clean peanuts. So she filled a few old pie tins with peanuts and placed them on the ground several steps away from the compost. The joy amongst the crows was evident from Loupe’s first caw to his peers. It was a demanding caw.

“Come now!” he seemed to call, “Come see!”

They came, they ate, they rejoiced, they fluffed their feathers to maximum fluffiness. They picked up the peanut shells in their shiny beaks, flew up to the power lines, and dropped them so they would crack open on the hot sidewalk, ready for consumption. The yard smelled like warm peanut butter and sounded like a celebration. From her creaky, plastic folding chair on the porch, Amalia watched the crows and felt as if she were hosting the world’s best party. Everyone was having a great time, and she didn’t have to make small talk with anyone.

After the peanuts, Amalia expanded to sunflower seeds and some sort of seed-brick that looked like a horrible granola bar, but which Adalberto, the whiskery feed-store owner, assured her the crows would like. She also bought dried mealworms, crispy chapulines, raisins, and fresh grapes, which were Loupe’s favorites. These treats never went on the compost pile; instead, she placed them in the pie tins that she attached to the top of a rusted café table that she’d dragged to the center of the yard when it became clear that the crows felt safer off the ground. Her café table was the life of the neighborhood.

She named more crows. Stumpy had one mangled foot. Chismosa never stopped squawking, regardless of whether anyone was listening, and regularly flew around with her mouth wide open. Sugar doled out affection left and right. Panzón ate with enthusiasm, evident in his thick torso. Eagle was invariably serious and judgmental, and he spent hours rubbing his beak back and forth on the power lines as though sharpening it.

When the crows began bringing her gifts, she knew they had named her in return. She would’ve given up her air conditioning for the whole summer to know what they called her.

Old-Food-Pile-Human? Ground-Based-Treat-Bringer? Earth-Bound-Crow-Worshipper? She smiled at the thought.

On the Sunday when César finally called and suggested a separation, the crows brought her their first gift: a shiny piece of plastic, a thick strip of tinsel that people put in their apricot trees to keep the birds away. The crows placed it in their empty pie dish on the rusty café table as if to say, “We are smarter than those people and those other birds.” Amalia took it inside and used a magnet to display it on her refrigerator, as she had done when her boys were little, their hot hands shoving papers at her, practically yelling, “Look what I made, Mama! Look, look!”

The crows’ gift was instead given in silence, like a test, to see if she would notice. Her joy about the gift bubbled inside her, and she wondered if she should be more upset about the separation, which she knew really meant divorce. Should she feel abandoned? Sinful? Sad? She felt around inside herself, searching, but she didn’t feel any of that. Looking at the glittering plastic stuck to her refrigerator, she just felt important.

Amalia began talking to the crows. They were talking to her, after all. It was only right to talk back.

“Hey, Loupe!” she would shout up at him as he rested on the telephone line in front of her house. “Loopy Loupe! I got some crunchy grapes for you at the market today!” Out the window, she might affectionately shout, “Chismosa! Your chisme is too loud! I’m trying to watch TV in here!”

By the time Amalia signed her divorce papers, nearly a year after César’s departure, she was convinced that many of the crows knew their names. It felt like progress, the measurable kind. It felt real.

The gifts continued, and she had to build a small altar in the living room on top of her grandmother’s old upright piano to display them. Four soda can tabs. Three screws. One playing card (a seven of clubs). Several food wrappers with shiny interiors. Two dented keys. Several beads. Five bent Jarritos tops. One small crystal. A quarter, a dime, and a 100-peso coin. Two earrings (not a matching set). One plastic gecko toy. A fake pearl hair clip. The silver cap of a lipstick tube. Each time, the crows put the gift in the empty pie dish. Just one gift at a time; they didn’t want to spoil her.

By autumn, the crows no longer feared Amalia. When she shuffled outside to leave some pea shells on the compost pile, they hopped out of her way, but few bothered flying up into the tree or onto the power lines anymore. She greeted them by name. They cawed and clicked back at her. She fed them the two roosters that had come from her batch of chicks, cleaning and cooking the carcasses first, of course. Only the best for her crows. This solved the cock-a-doodle-doo problem with her neighbors, and the crows seemed delighted since they were voracious omnivores. She imagined they also enjoyed consuming their competition for her avian affection.

With the rooster issue fixed, the neighbors began complaining about the crows. She got an earful about it from both Mr. and Mrs. Hernandez when she was fetching the mail. The crows were too loud, too messy, and “a little creepy,” they said. Amalia told them to park in their junk-filled garage if they didn’t like caca on their cars, and then she laughed and walked back to her porch. César, who always believed in “keeping the peace,” would’ve been appalled. Amalia settled into her plastic chair, cinched the too-short belt on her cotton bathrobe, wiggled her tiny toes, and returned to shucking peas with the crows, Loupe standing vigilantly on the low porch wall beside her like a living gargoyle.

Amalia’s younger son, David, visited in the early winter and marveled at her crows. He watched his squat little mother from inside the house as she fed them, chatting to them nonstop as she unpinned sun-bleached laundry from the clothesline, as she walked across the yard to feed her hens, and as she shuffled to her mailbox on the sidewalk. The crows regarded David with suspicion, mistrust, and an obvious fear that he was going to interrupt their routine. He didn’t. He came and went, telling his mother she was becoming “some kind of bird witch” in her old age.

“Works for me,” she had replied breezily. He’d expected to find her shaken at the loss of her marriage, but instead he discovered that she had grown particular about what was allowed in the refrigerator (no beer!) and where food scraps went (not in the trash!). She’d admonished him when he put banana peels on the compost pile, saying, “No, no, Davey. They hate banana peels. They will pull those peels out of the pile and leave them all over the yard.” Confused, David asked, “Who will?”

“My crows!” Amalia replied with exasperation, gesturing to the front yard with both hands to make her point. David followed her gesture with his gaze and saw no fewer than fifteen crows in the yard, on the fence, on the phone lines, and standing atop a rusty café table.

At the airport, David called his big brother, Martin. He didn’t bother with small talk, instead stating immediately, “Marty, man. Mama is getting so weird. She named all the crows, and she buys them treats. Treats, man! Remember when she wouldn’t even buy us Fruit by the Foot?!”

But Martin just laughed his slow laugh and said, “Cálmate, little brother. Relax, she’s probably just lonely without Dad.”

But Amalia was not lonely. Her collection of gifts grew. Adalberto from the feed store ordered special treats for her crows. Kids stopped on the street to watch her feed them, giggling, their dark eyes shining with the young wonder derived from seeing something for the first time. They’d seen crows and ravens and roadrunners their whole lives, but now they saw those birds anew. It was as though Amalia had peeled the birds like black fruit, revealing that they held sparks of magic inside, hidden just beneath their feathers.

When school started in the fall, the children began stopping at her gate nearly every weekday during their walk home, saving snacks from their lunches to share with her crows. The young audience called her Tía Crow, or sometimes Títi Cuervo, and they gasped when Loupe landed on her shoulder, and they laughed when Chismosa performed the Peanuts-Are-Delicious Dance, mouth open, comically kicking up spirals of fine dirt. Amalia and the crows were the best entertainment in the neighborhood. All the kids said so.

In the last bit of that winter, when the sun shone daily but the thin air refused to hold any heat, Sugar and Panzón disappeared with a few younger crows. Amalia worried. Had they grown sick, gotten lost, died in a storm, joined a crow commune? Not being able to ask the survivors pinched at her. She gave the remaining crows extra treats. Nearly all of the crows took peanuts from her hands now, and the old regulars were downright affectionate, but Eagle would never even consider such a thing, and he clearly judged his compatriots harshly for fawning over a human. Amalia could almost hear him thinking: sycophants, sell-outs, suck- ups! You shame the Noble House of Crow! Eagle took himself too seriously; it amused both Amalia and Loupe endlessly.

Amalia’s collection of gifts deepened. A dried, white vertebra. A laminated baseball card with milky, curling edges. A snail shell. Two sparkling black arrowheads. A collection of smooth, polished pebbles that she eventually recognized as part of the gravel from a yard renovation a few streets over. Amalia did not return the polished gravel pieces to the neighbors’ yard. The treasures all went atop the piano, where she laid them out like a mandala. Each new gift meant rearranging all the others, a meditative act, creating an ofrenda for her living self. She thought of it sometimes as the altar to me.

The days were always sunny, and the crows kept her company when she was home, which was most of the time. When she was indoors, Loupe sometimes landed on her windowsill to ask for food, or maybe just to check on her. Amalia had happily retired from her job at the middle school cafeteria three years ago, but in the spring, she began working one day per week at the feed store when Adalberto, in a parched whisper, asked her if she was interested. He was old and wanted a day off. Plus, she got an employee discount, and she liked the sort of folks that visited the feed store. Most were quiet and knew what they wanted, but a few asked her interesting questions that she knew the answers to: When would there be more baby chicks in stock? Can you keep chickens and turkeys in the same coop? How can you get cholla out of goat fur? No one ever asked about crows.

One day after coming home from a quiet shift at the feed store, she found a small ring in the center of the empty pie dish on the rusty café table. It was a gold ring, with a single clear stone, so dusty that she took it inside to wash it with dish soap. It looks like an engagement ring, she thought, an old one, the kind from her parents’ generation, not like these new rings with so many stones. A simple gold band with just one perfect, circular diamond, made to last, made to keep.

She’d never gotten a diamond ring from César; instead, she’d gotten pregnant and married fast, a plain silver band on her finger and a promise of something better someday. But Amalia had insisted they not waste money on another ring. Spend it on the boys, the house, the groceries, the health insurance, the new roof, the baseball uniforms, the plumber, the transmission; she’d insisted. There were always more practical ways to spend any few dollars that they managed to save. The silver band was “good enough,” she’d said. César, never a romantic about anything other than baseball, was pleased to agree with her about the ring.

Amalia slid the clean ring onto her ring finger and was surprised to find it fit just right. Tight enough not to fall off, but not so tight that it made her short finger look like a tiny sausage. She held her hand out and looked at it. The gold shone, making the skin of her hand appear rich and warm. The stone blinked alive in the light, sparkling.

Amalia’s breath had gotten stuck in her lungs, and she pushed it out in an audible “woosh” as she realized with astonishment that she actually had wanted a real ring all these many years. She had wanted to feel intentionally chosen, like a first pick, a top priority, a prize. All her life, she prided herself on being pragmatic, but now, as she scrutinized her bejeweled hand, she came face-to-face (or face-to-hand?) with some ignored piece of herself that wanted to feel cherished, worthy, even a little spoiled.

Amalia coughed, her eyes watered and dripped, and she laughed aloud at herself. Crying over a crow-gifted ring! She hadn’t even cried over the divorce. She hadn’t even cried during confession when she had to tell the Padre about her divorce. But this? This makes her cry?! She laughed even louder at her crazy self.

“Caw,” she heard from the open window, “Caw! Caw!” It was Loupe, bending his neck side to side, regarding her intently with one eye, then the other. She twisted her hand around to show him the ring, wiggling her fingers daintily, like a cartoon princess.

“Thank you,” she said gently, her words carrying through the window screen. “I love it.” Loupe watched her for a few more seconds before jumping off the sill and into the air, where he ascended to his usual perch on the power line. He looked secure and relaxed, a crow “about his business,” as her boys would say. Smiling, she wiped the tears that dripped from her nose and hung on the soft skin of her jaw.

Amalia went to the kitchen to wash her hands and some fresh grapes, noting with pleasure how the ring sparkled in the faucet water, catching the desert sun shining in through the window above the sink, peppering the tile countertop with dashes of white light and tiny rainbows.

pieces.html:
From: Bec Halloran (bechalloran82@aol.com)
To: Genevieve Halloran (ghallor@fas.harvard.edu)
Date: March 1996
Subject: GUESS WHAT

Gen!!! We have email at school and I made Mom get AOL at home too. Dad took three hours to install it and now nobody’s allowed to use the phone, in case the internet needs it. How’s Harvard? The parental units can’t stop bragging about you. Dad has a Harvard sweatshirt for the gym and a second, better Harvard sweatshirt for church. Mrs. Enright says my math is almost as good as yours, so maybe I’ll be there one day too. Ha ha.

Also, and I am NOT making a big deal of this, Theo Pritchard asked me to the Spring Fling. Theo Pritchard, Gen. He asked me by the dumpsters, which I’ve decided is romantic. I said yes, obviously, but I was extremely casual. I waited almost four seconds. I wish you were here to do my hair. Mom always makes the left side bigger.

Bec xx

From: Genevieve
Subject: Re: GUESS WHAT

Darling, how wonderful. Of course you’ll be here one day. Mrs. Enright said almost exactly the same thing about my math, and look what happened, so I think we can trust her. Theo is a lovely boy. I remember his older brother Julian, who took me to senior prom and wrote to me for some years afterwards from West Point, rather beautifully, until I asked him to stop. I was told he thereafter requested the furthest posting the Army offers, out of despair. I hope Theo has the same beautiful manners.

Wear the blue dress. Let Mom do the hair. The left side settles by itself once you’re dancing, and she’ll remember doing it for years. I’ll be thinking of you.

G x

From: Bec
Date: May 2000
Subject: PRESIDENT. also PROM QUEEN. in the same WEEK.

Gen. I’m student body co-president with Therese. The votes were exactly tied, which is lucky, because she’s my best friend and we’ve already worked out custody of the gavel. I get weekends. AND I’m Junior Prom Queen! Mrs. Delgado says nobody has done the double since 1976. There’s a sash and a tiara that has been repaired, I think, with gum. Mom cried at both events and Dad filmed the wrong family for ten minutes at the coronation.

Mom put an empty chair beside her for you, although I told her a federal judge doesn’t give his clerk the night off for a tiara. It held Dad’s coat, which was nearly as pleased as you would’ve been.

Bec xx

From: Genevieve
Subject: Re: PRESIDENT. also PROM QUEEN. in the same WEEK.

My darling girl. The gavel and the tiara in one week. I laughed and cried, remembering how I ran for president unopposed, which was even lonelier than it sounds, and how I withdrew from the prom court on principle, because the voting set girls against one another (feminist principles, social justice, etc., etc.). The school paper covered my position rather more than I wanted. There was an editorial. You get to enjoy your sash uncomplicated by principles. In many ways that’s sweeter.

I wish I could have seen Dad filming the Massies. I told the Judge your news. He said hm, which from him is a standing ovation. Thank Mom for the chair. Dad’s coat has always been a very supportive garment.

G x

From: Bec
Date: December 2000
Subject: ok don’t make this about Harvard

YALE. I got into YALE, Gen. Early. Dad has bought the car sticker, the sweatshirt, the scarf, and a pennant, and we don’t own a wall prepared to receive it, because the wall is full of Harvard. I waited until after dinner in case you called, but Mom said the Supreme Court had something on this week and the clerks weren’t being let out.

Anyway. Yale. Your little sister. I can’t feel my hands.

Bec xx

From: Genevieve
Subject: Re: ok don’t make this about Harvard

Yale! Bec! They’ll adore you. It’s such a friendly place. I had three very happy years across the street at the law school, where I tried never to mention where I’d been before, and everyone was kind enough to find out anyway. The pizza on Wooster Street is better than anything in Cambridge, which I used to say in the dining hall just to watch people’s faces. You’ll hear there’s a rivalry. Pay it no attention. Harvard people are insufferable about it, and I say that as one of them, technically. I’ve always found the number-one business rather vulgar.

I’m sorry I didn’t call. We’ve had rather a week here. I can’t say anything about it, except that I did suggest another way of doing things, and they were very nice about it.

Buy Dad the wall. He’s earned it. I’ll call on Sunday.

G x

From: Bec
Date: March 2005
Subject: HARVARD LAW. SIT DOWN.

HARVARD LAW, GEN. The fat envelope. I opened it in the driveway and screamed so loudly the Patels called to make sure nobody had been run over. Your little sister is going to Harvard Law School. I’ve been saying Juris Doctor in a voice I’d been saving for movie trailers. Dad says that for once the wall can stay as it is.

Do you remember sitting on the landing outside my door the night before I started high school, because I said I couldn’t breathe? I thought of that in the driveway. Then I screamed again.

Bec xx

From: Genevieve
Subject: Re: HARVARD LAW. SIT DOWN.

The fat envelope in the driveway. Bec, this is one of the happiest emails I’ve ever received. Harvard Law will give you scale, argument, those gorgeous gloomy libraries. When I turned it down for Yale, the Dean wrote me rather a wounded letter, and people behaved as though I’d done something radical, but rankings never entered my mind. I wanted somewhere small enough that they don’t give grades. They don’t believe in them there. You will be given grades, Bec, a great many, and I think that will be lovely for you. Rankings are noise, darling. Let them be noise for you too, if you can.

I remember the landing. You breathed perfectly once you fell asleep. I stayed anyway. Scream in as many driveways as you like. You’ve earned every scream.

G x

From: Bec
Date: February 2016
Subject: you are looking at a PARTNER

Youngest partner in the firm’s history, Gen. Harcourt, Pell & Strand. They announced it at the partners’ retreat and Martin from Restructuring did a spit-take with a LaCroix. I have a corner office. It faces a wall, but it’s a corner.

I called Mom, then Dad, who was in the same room as Mom but wanted his own call, then Richard, who said good job in the voice he uses for the dog. Then I stared at your name for a while and decided to email, because you always answer email.

Bec xx

From: Genevieve
Subject: Re: you are looking at a PARTNER

Partner at Harcourt, Pell & Strand. I’m so proud I could burst. After my year at the Court, and then the two arguments there, private practice felt like a room I’d already walked around, which is why I went to the Solicitor General’s office instead, and why I change the subject whenever anyone says the word confirmation. I’ve never had a corner. The government gives you a window with the Washington Monument in it and expects you to manage. You’re still discovering the room, Bec. That joy is the real wealth, and nobody announces it at a retreat.

A corner that faces a wall still knows it’s a corner. Martin sounds like a treasure. Guard him.

I always answer you.

G x

From: Bec
Date: May 2018
Subject: small announcement, huge kid

Lily read a whole chapter book. She’s FIVE, Gen. Her teacher used the words off the charts, and I’ve repeated them, casually, to forty people, including a stranger in line at the post office. Also she made the travel soccer team, the one for eight-year-olds. I’m not saying prodigy. I’m just leaving the word on the table.

She asked whether Aunt Gen was coming to field day. I said maybe next year, which isn’t technically a lie, because there’s always another next year until there isn’t.

Bec xx

From: Genevieve
Subject: Re: small announcement, huge kid

Lily is extraordinary and I’ve printed this for the fridge. Don’t compare her with the twins, because every child unfolds to their own clock. Sebastian only played Carnegie Hall because his cello teacher insisted. I thought nine was too young, and said so, to Carnegie Hall. Odette’s Mandarin is only fluent because of the immersion school. It’s environment, Bec, purely environment. Lily has something rarer, which is your fire.

Tell her Aunt Gen is trying for next year. The Hague has swallowed June again. I did raise field day with the International Court of Justice, and they were very nice about it.

G x

From: Bec
Date: July 2024
Subject: divorce final / new person??? / life is insane

Divorce is final. Richard kept the Peloton and frankly good riddance to both. I didn’t tell you during the bad part. I wanted at least one thing in the email I could type in capitals.

AND. I’ve met someone. Tom. Retired tech billionaire, sold the company in the spring, and Gen, I’m underselling it the way he does. He was on magazine covers and now he restores wooden boats in Maine, drives a Volvo wagon with 180,000 miles on it, and read my favorite book without being asked. He has forearms like a public health warning. I’m forty-two and giddy. Is that allowed?

Bec xx

From: Genevieve
Subject: Re: divorce final / new person??? / life is insane

Allowed? Darling, it’s compulsory. My second marriage, to Anneke, taught me that the second is the one you choose with your whole education. Anneke had a certain amount of money when we met, and we gave it away, mostly, which I mention only so you know it can be done. There’s a hospital wing somewhere. We asked them not to. Tom sounds splendid. A billionaire in a Volvo wagon has passed the only means test that matters, and a man who restores boats understands patience, water, and rot, which is everything a marriage needs.

I’m sorry about the bad part, my love. You could have told me without capitals.

Giddiness at forty-two is wisdom wearing a party hat. Enjoy him. Marry him. Let Dad film it.

G x

From: Bec
Date: September 2026
Subject: Gen. GEN. Sit down.

Gen, it’s confirmed. Literally. The Senate voted this afternoon and I’m going to the United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit. Judge Halloran. There’ll be a robe, an investiture, and Tom has asked whether he may whittle me a gavel. I explained that appellate judges don’t really use them, there are three of us up there and nobody bangs anything. He said that sounded like a gap in the system.

I haven’t told Mom yet. You were first.

And I’ll say it. The wedding last spring, where Dad filmed forty minutes of a caterer and your chair had the coat on it again, because Mom said you were on a retreat and I assumed she meant the kind with a keynote. The Second Circuit this fall. Lily starting at Princeton at fourteen, which means I now say the word prodigy at the post office, unprompted, and Dad is pricing a second wall. I have every one of these emails in a folder called Gen, and in thirty years you’ve never once written first. I keep waiting for the reply where you sat on the Second Circuit before it existed, or turned down the Supreme Court because the robes were itchy. Go on. I’m braced. It’s tradition at this point, and I’d miss it.

Judge Bec xx

From: Genevieve (now sending from sister.karuna@plumhollow.org)
Subject: Re: Gen. GEN. Sit down.

My dearest Bec,

Judge Halloran. I read your email four times and each time the useless whittled gavel made me weep with happiness. Tell Tom it’ll be the thing you reach for first.

You’re waiting for me to reach past you one final time, and I want to be honest, because you’ve earned honesty at the appellate level. I can’t do it. You have outrun me, darling, comprehensively, a robe and a billionaire and a fourteen-year-old at Princeton, and it’s glorious to watch. That isn’t the reason, though. Last fall, after the twins left for college, I set the whole ladder down.

It wasn’t the kind of retreat with a keynote. I live now at Plum Hollow Buddhist Priory in Vermont. Anneke has the house and the dog and comes on visiting Sundays, and says she has never seen me so pleased with myself, which the abbess says is something to work with. They’ve given me a new name, Sister Karuna, which means compassion. I haven’t earned it, though the abbess says the not-having-earned-it is the practice. I keep the garden, badly, and I’m getting worse, which I’m told is progress. I let achievement go like a bird I’d held too tightly for forty years, and Bec, my hands have never felt so light. Titles, honors, cases, the Latin on my degrees: I look at them now the way you’d look at a beautiful coat in a country where you no longer feel the cold.

They let you bring one box. I brought our emails, printed out and tied with a blue ribbon. There you all are: the blue dress, the sash, Dad’s coat in my chair, the wall with no room for the pennant, the driveway, the corner, Lily’s chapter book, Tom’s boats. You’re right that I never wrote first. I was always waiting for you. And I never came, did I. I told myself it was the Judge, and then the Court, and then The Hague, but I think the truth is that I never learned how to sit in a chair and only watch. It’s most of what they teach here. I’m bottom of the class, which is new. Don’t ever think I didn’t see you, though. I saw every step.

And I should tell you, because you’d hear it from Mom and she’ll get the details wrong, that last month I took the bodhisattva vow. People usually wait years to be allowed. The abbess said that in my case there seemed no point. I have promised to remain in this earthly plane of suffering until every last sentient being reaches enlightenment before me. Do you understand what I’m telling you, Bec? My welfare now comes behind that of ALL beings. Behind every slug in my lettuces. Behind every man who has ever explained to me a case I argued. Behind, and I made the abbess be precise about this, whoever invented reply-all, in this life and the next. Behind Richard. Behind Richard’s Peloton. I go last, darling. Out of everything. Last. It’s the lowest place there is, and I confess that from down here the view is rather wonderful.

But you still feel the cold, my love, and the coat is magnificent on you. Wear the robe.

I’m so proud of you. I have always been proud of you. Pride is one of the attachments I’ve released, of course, but I kept a little back in a jar, like the garden honey. It’s yours.

May all beings be free of suffering,

Sister Karuna (your Gen) x

P.S. The White House did call, two years ago, about the other Court. The robes aren’t itchy, darling. They’re heavy, which is worse. I mention it only for the folder.

pieces.html:
My dad got a job in Chattanooga so my parents are moving
away from the house where they raised me. I went home
(from Raleigh where I live by myself) and my brother went home
(from college) to celebrate Dad
or were we grievers? Who put down what they hold
and go home always.

Dad lined up fourteen almost-empty liquor bottles
on the sideboard in the dining room for us to drink
so they won’t have to roll around in a moving truck.
Our family dog (Harley) is ashes in a Ziploc bag in the dining room too.
She’s been there for going on three years and Dad said
see this is why it was such a smart move not to bury her
in this backyard. There would have been no visiting her any longer
and he wants her in the yard of his Forever Home.

Mom asked when she dies
is he going to carry her around in a Ziploc bag
until he gets to his Forever Home? and Dad said probably yes and kept talking
but Mom didn’t want Harley ashed in the first place.
She wanted to bury the dog in the backyard
where there used to be an oak tree which my brother thwacked
my sparkly green plastic baton against when we were five and seven
and it broke. She looked at me while Dad kept talking to my brother
or to the fourteen liquor bottles and said she thinks it’s like in the Bible—

when we return to dust we shouldn’t be dead in a Ziploc bag
we should be in the ground where we came from.
But the tree isn’t there any longer and next we won’t be.
I said to my brother which of the fourteen liquor bottles
do you think Dad should put Harley in to get her to the Forever Home?
He right away picked an orange glass bottle of pineapple rum.
Dad said it’s from the Bahamas and probably twenty-five years old
which makes it older than me and by far than the dog.

In my head we took shots until we were dizzy and watched the sun shine
through the colored glass bottles. Outside the window
is a blueberry bush we picked clean every year I was growing.
It has bird netting over it but usually the birds got under the net and thrashed.
In my head we curled up under the dining room table with the empty bottles
and cried and cried.

Next we won’t be here and that kid who cried over the plastic baton is
ashes in a Ziploc bag. Not in that dining room
but somewhere behind my eyes where I can carry her to my Forever Home.
Ashes in a heavy orange bottle where there used to be pineapple rum.

pieces.author: Jack Godby
pieces.bio: Jack Godby is an emerging writer from South London. His short fiction explores the true and untrue of contemporary British society.

pieces.html:
At some point in the late nineties, all of the Little Old Ladies disappeared. Evidence that they had even existed at all, however, didn’t surface until much later—indeed, it took thirty years for anyone to realise that an entire generation of women had seemingly vanished. The general consensus now is that they left in the middle of the night, so as not to make a fuss.

It took society a long time to conclude that something was a bit off as the clues came slowly and weren’t immediately obvious: the discovery of a dog-eared family photograph in which a mysterious wrinkled figure dozes in a corner armchair, a divorcee despising her ex-partner but treasuring the wedding ring without knowing why, a young man’s half-formed memory of something musty and sweet.

For purposes of clarity, the definition of “Little Old Lady” is important here, for it is not simply a signifier of age. Today there are “old” women in the chronological sense; however, these are of a different sort altogether, and are often indistinguishable from their younger counterparts.

Characterised by shin-length skirts, tartan trolleys, and hair worn in short “sets” (a style with the appearance of balled candy floss), it was perhaps the colour of the hair that initially bemused historians the most. Although shocking by modern standards, relinquishing to the unwanted effects of age was a central tenet of the subculture—and this went beyond hair colour alone. Particularly striking recollections recount “skin that was almost see-through in places, but hung loosely in others . . . it bunched up around the finger-joints like old tights.” Accounts such as these may be judged as obscene today, but the commitment to anti-aestheticism must surely be commended.

Initial theories regarding their disappearance included the idea that they were all put in care homes and isolated from wider society. This theory fell out of favour, however, as no one was interested enough to visit one and check. Following this, it was widely agreed for a time that the Little Old Ladies must simply have died off during the winter months.

It wasn’t until the fortuitous discovery of a dusty tin labelled “Rover Assorted Biscuits” at the back of a kitchen cupboard that we were able to glean more insight. Inside the tin was a postcard—one side featuring a faded image of sheer white cliffs, and on the other, a handwritten message. The now-famous note reads:

Dearest Catherine,

I’m going to see the sea with my girlfriends, and then on to see your father—how I’ve missed him! Don’t worry about me, you’ve got better things to think about! There’ll be bluebirds flying over the cliffs of Dover tomorrow, just you wait and see.

Love you, Mum.

P.S. I’ve left you a little something, get yourself something nice.

Also in the tin was a five-pound note. It is unlikely that the named “Catherine” saw the note, and it is unknown whether she ever realised her mother had gone.

Tickets for “Little Old Ladies” (London Museum, September 1st to March 30th) go on sale June 1st. Admission is £15; unfortunately, we are unable to offer concessionary rates at this time.

pieces.title: Silt
pieces.author: Aardhra Chandran
pieces.html:
By morning the river has withdrawn,
leaving a black tidemark on the walls.
A child’s primer lies open in the courtyard,
its alphabet running quietly into mud.

On the high verandah, three deeds dry
beneath the ceiling fan. Their embossed seals
remain raised above the softened paper,
small islands refusing the water.

Down the lane, a mattress hangs
over the boundary wall,
brown water threading through its cotton
and darkening the hibiscus below.

He turns the pressure cooker over.
River ash has silvered its belly.
Inside the rubber gasket,
a dead frog has folded itself small.

At the relief office, wet clothes steam
beside kerosene, river weed, and sweat.
The clerk asks for proof of residence.
Behind him, his house is drying.

His photograph on the form has lost
the roof, the mango tree, the blue gate.
A purple thumbprint blooms beside it,
slowly taking the shape of a country.

Outside, bottled water waits in crates,
clear enough to show every bubble.
By evening, buses return to the road.
The fare has risen by two rupees.

His daughter counts the coins twice
before climbing aboard with her books.
At home, she kneels in the doorway
and rubs mud from her name.

The first letter loosens beneath her nail.
The rest has entered the brick.

That night, the refrigerator starts humming.
A single drop falls from the ceiling
into the steel bowl they have kept beneath it.
The bowl fills with nothing but the sound.
