Birthday parties are as inevitable as death and taxes, in his line of work.

Today, the balloons are bright and the sky is reflective and the kids are screaming and the cake is wilting under the heat and the kids are still screaming. Hundreds of them. No, that’s an exaggeration. Dozens, then.

The face paint on Andrew’s cheek is mildly claustrophobic, too—its clamminess heavy as the artist continues to add layers. So Andrew breathes in. Breathes out. Swallows past the smell of sugar and pepperoni and overheating bounce house plastic. He looks for his wife, who ditched him a half hour ago.

They’d expressly agreed Not to Ditch Each Other and to head out once the cake was cut. But these parties have a way of drawing people apart. Now, Sophie is standing forty feet to his right, just out of reach of the shade and his pleas.

She smiles and nods to another mom, all while swaying under the onslaught of preschoolers threatening to take her out at the knee. He would say she deserves it, but he loves her.

He, meanwhile, is balancing on a too-small chair while his son watches.

“Handsome, Daddy,” his four-year-old son beams, ants in his pants. The very son who convinced him to visit the face-painting tent.

“All done,” the artist says, handing him a mirror. “What do you think?”

That I look like an asshole. “It’s great,” he responds before even seeing his reflection. Then, he catches a glimpse. “I . . .” He turns his head this way, that way. Rolls his neck. Straightens his shoulders. Andrew had pointed to the first sample picture on the board in the face-painting tent, and now . . .

“You a prince, Daddy!”

He supposes he is. He offers the artist a smile and the mirror, and she curtsies. Her cheeks flush pink.

Andrew stands from the chair, his back ramrod. He takes measured steps toward his wife. His son bounces at his heels.

“Looking good, Andrew,” shouts a passerby.

Andrew dips his head, then continues his promenade across the yard.

He reaches his wife and, instinctually, she welcomes him with a hand to his forearm. Then double-takes.

“Andy,” she breathes, a nervous giggle hidden in her words. “You? Where have you been?” She sounds as if she’s just run a mile, her chest rising and falling. Her gaze sweeps his face, then settles on his eyes.

“Oh, I . . .”

The other woman interjects: “You have to share your skincare routine. You look about ten years younger than the last time I saw you. Glowing.” She exhales, a hand to her chest.

Andrew squints and purses his lips, unsure if she’s being facetious. “What do I use, babe?” he asks his wife.

Sophie doesn’t take her eyes off him. “Just this stuff I saw on TikTok. I can send you a link.” Then to Andrew: “You do look . . . different. More . . .”

“Well, I’m royalty now, so, yeah?”

“Yeah?” She shakes the question from her head.

As soon as the other woman leaves, Sophie reaches up on tiptoes to whisper in his ear. “You’re so handsome, Andy. I don’t think I tell you that enough.”

The party continues with the usual beats—games, pizza, presents—but he relaxes into it. The other parents make their way over one by one to say hello. He waves a hand. Nods his head. Entertains their greetings.

And true to their word, Andrew, Sophie, and the children leave promptly after cake, Sophie’s arm linked with Andrew’s all the way to the car, like they’re newlyweds again. He waits until the kids are buckled in, then kisses her against the hatchback. He wipes a smudge of blue paint from her cheek before climbing into the car himself.

This weekend, the party is for his seven-year-old daughter’s friend, so there are considerably fewer dinosaurs and substantially more tiaras. Andrew watches his daughter get a unicorn horn swiped across her freckled forehead, the pinks amalgamating.

He asks if it’d be OK if he had a turn. If there are no kids waiting, of course. It’s just for fun.

This artist acquiesces with a smirk, and Andrew tells her what he’d like. When he peers into the mirror five minutes later and sees the red and black paint of a superhero, his muscles flex themselves. Sophie steps up behind him and traces her fingers across the small of his back.

“When did you start working out again?” she teases with a smile and a squeeze on his defined shoulder.

Her pupils dilate when she catches their shared reflection.

His voice turns deep, gruff. “All the better to save you with.”

Sophie’s fingers cling to his shirt and dig into his skin. Before she can answer, Andrew notices movement on the edge of his vision. It’s a reflex, the way his arm flashes out to catch the falling child.

This pint-sized human would have tumbled straight into the concrete, bare knees and ice cream be damned, if Andrew hadn’t been right there, thank God—Sophie recounts her husband’s prowess to anyone who will listen. A savior.

Later, when Andrew overhears the birthday girl’s father discussing the pizza pickup, he offers to assist. He carries nine pies from a trunk to a folding table. His arms ripple. The other guests gasp, and their hands itch to applaud.

During presents, Andrew watches a young guest—someone’s preteen brother—attempt to snatch a newly opened toy from the pile. He’s there like lightning, his hand coming between the boy and the remote-control convertible. The boy’s father thanks Andrew for stepping in with his wayward son.

Andrew’s body is invigorated. His focus is sharp. His only mission left? Bath and bed for the kids before 8 p.m.. Because Sophie needs him.

He carries her to the car, crossing-the-threshold style, while the kids trail behind shrieking and whooping. She’s giggling, too, burying her face in his straining chest.

At home, mission accomplished, Andrew pins his wife against the wall with his hips. She runs her hands down his sides.

“With great power comes great responsibility,” he rumbles against her neck, before he makes love to her with gravity-defying feats of strength and stamina.

When he finally takes his own shower and sees his clean, smooth face through the fog, he senses an absence. He sighs, and his veins and straining muscles deflate with the exhale.

Another party for his daughter’s circle, and, since this is a real sophisticated soiree, there are two face painters. Andrew won’t have to wait long for a turn, so he lets his son go first.

He chooses a pirate this time, wondering what a little rebellion will feel like on his skin.

He keeps his mischief in check throughout the party, only stealing two extra cupcakes to bring home. He knows he’ll be hungry after he plunders Sophie’s treasure. She might be, too, actually. He swipes a third.

The other parents give his dark swagger a wide berth out of respect. But not his wife. She’s holding a sweating soda and eyeing Andrew from across the lawn, her straw always just out of reach of her searching lips because she can’t bother to tear her eyes away from him to find it.

He notices a few of the other dads have colorful cheeks and foreheads, too—scorpions, dinosaurs, and panthers, the paint overwhelming their features—while their wives titter with Sophie. She must have let them in on their secret, and the other couples were brave enough to try it.

When the party ends, Sophie scurries to him, and he hoists her over his shoulder. It’s only a few blocks’ walk home, so he carries her the whole way. The kids have run ahead of them this time, chanting a sea shanty they made up that’s also suspiciously reminiscent of a famous theme park ride.

Row, row, the sea is calling;

We want treasure! We row till morning;

Yo-ho, yo-ho, we’re a pirate family!

Dinner is a feast of cured meat, cheese, crusty bread, and chicken nuggets, drowned with ale and sparkling water from goblets dug out of the hutch. The kids continue with their shanties through bathtime. Sophie swishes her skirts and beckons Andrew to the bedroom with a crooked finger.

The stolen cupcakes, slightly squished, fuel them.

When the next weekend is absent of a party, Andrew’s cheeks are itchingly dry. His jawline seems inordinately weak. He almost considers a trip to the local craft store to see if they carry face paint. He does check online. But, alas, they don’t have it, and Amazon will take three days to deliver, and by that point it will almost be another weekend and another party, and . . .

He doesn’t have to wait long. The preschool is hosting a family carnival, and one of the teachers is filling the role of artist. After watching a few paint jobs, though, Andrew volunteers to do his own.

He browses the sample photos, though he’s already certain what he’s in the mood for. The jungle-themed party all but cements his decision, with images of the equator’s variegated fauna and wildlife inspiring him. Yet it’s a different variegation that ends up catching his curiosity—that of a tabby cat. Really, a kitten. He could be so playful; his tongue so rough; his footfalls soft. What if . . .

He glances toward his wife. Sophie is watching him, licking her lips.

So, instead, he becomes power and potent energy.

In his tiger form, he stalks through the party, lithe and smooth, sensing and scenting the crowd. His teeth are long, and his claws are sharpened to points. He looks for threats, and, finding none, takes to basking in the courtyard’s sun. The fathers watch him, even attempt to mimic his electric nonchalance in their get-ups. Andrew broadens his shoulders, giving them a good view.

This time when Sophie joins him, she, too, is painted. He quirks his head, taking in her pink and gold tiara, the swirls across her temples. His heart races. His eyebrows twitch. In all his coolness, he sidles up to her. She is his princess. He, her fierce protector.

The crowd around them almost cheers, though the other women are more concerned with rushing to join the line for their own flowery paint—now that it’s clearly de rigueur.

When Andrew and Sophie meet in carnal pleasure later that night, he consumes her. Devours her in all her softness. She lets him feast.

After, when he uses a damp cloth to wipe the paint from her body and his own, an odd sense of insatiate hunger gurgles beneath the relief of shrinking limbs.

Following the positive reception, Sophie has the enthusiastic idea to learn from YouTube videos, so they can spend their weeknights, too, donned in colors. Andrew, a bear; Sophie, a flower. He, a lion; she, a mouse. A beast and a damsel. Or a tentacled sea monster, with extra dexterity to take out the trash and grab her ass in one pass. It’s intoxicating—motivating—the way she bows under his touch or a glance.

The kids ignore them, as long as they’re fed and bathed and have clean clothes. He assumes they’re getting their homework done. If he’s not working or checking his email for birthday e-vites, he’s thinking of animals and reminding himself of the way Sophie’s doe eyes darken when she sees his manliness take shape.

Their colors change with the seasons, and Sophie decides that, this year, they will host a New Year’s block party. They develop a plan—just the right idea, they assure each other giddily: invite their neighbors and friends from their children’s schools, and hire a top artist to travel all the way from The City. They will be celebrated for their ingenuity!

While the town’s brood of youngsters dance in a cacophony of sparklers and bang snaps, men and women snake around their court, waiting for a turn in the artist’s chair. They huddle against each other to ward against the cold and conspire on their designs. A few of the men even shout barbs down the line—taunts to each other about who will be fiercest or the most virile. The wives demure behind shy eyes and hummed laughs.

Andrew smirks. He, who has bestowed this gift to his neighbors, who has allowed them this chance to enter the new year in a new form, is confident in his choice. Though a rainbow of fireworks caught his attention initially, the menacing flames that now encircle his eyes will light up the night brighter than any glittery spectacle.

He searches for Sophie to show her. And to feed his fire with her oxygen. He sees her down the block, her back to him. In an instant, he’s there, spinning her toward him, not hiding his plans to engulf her.

Instead, when he sees what she’s done, the conflagration travels down his whole chest. Its embers sit low in his belly, in his flesh even absent of paint.

Silver threads fan out across her brow, ladder down her nose, kiss her lips, trace the lines of her jaw and neck. From one temple, a dense, black body lies in wait, its articulated legs—all eight—stretch across her forehead and cheek. One gets lost in the crease of her eyelid.

“Sophie,” he exhales. He almost tastes the bittersweetness of bait.

“I thought the colors would match . . . for later,” she says, and he knows. The black nightgown with silver threads that she saves for special occasions—the one she wore for his birthday last year.

Andrew studies her. He traces a finger across each filament. “Black widows eat their mates.”

Sophie’s hand flies to her mouth, but she can’t hide her blush.

He draws her fingers away and leans down to her ear. “I’m not scared.”

Their neighbors’ deferential hush at seeing this peculiar match-up speaks volumes.

When the ball has dropped, when the neighbors have left, when all the hot chocolate has been drunk, and the artist tipped handsomely, Sophie lures Andrew to her web.

Seeking more, more, more, they push the boundaries of what they thought they knew. Every evening, when Andrew steps through the door from work, he takes stock of his thrumming heart. He settles the children in front of the TV. Then, he and Sophie slough their daywear to reveal a matched fierceness: a shark churning in stormy waves, or wolves stalking each other. She’s a python undulating through their shared space. He’s a piranha, quick and sharp. These new beings keep them up till the earliest hours. And when his alarm blares at 6 a.m. each morning, the tedium of attiring himself in the shell of a middle-aged financial analyst makes Andrew’s skin crawl.

At a birthday party in the spring (who cares whose), Andrew enters through the flap of a white tent. He absorbs the portraits of great heroes and cartoon royalty, of renowned desert animals and the ocean’s most majestic creatures. Forest nymphs model in gilt frames. As has become custom now at these get-togethers, inspirations line the plastic walls—palaces erected solely for artists to exact transformations. Andrew’s lungs welcome the invasion of clay and chemical chalk. He breathes it into his metamorphosis.

The artist guides him to a silver chair in the corner. It’s just the two of them inside the opaque, flapping structure. He knows Sophie is next door making her choice. They had let all the other partygoers mutate first, as they prefer to emerge, alchemized, to a captive audience no longer impatient for a turn.

As he sits, his eye catches a luna moth, painted to extravagance, near one of the tent’s folds. It’s almost dragon-like in its coloration and shape. The subtlety of it nudges at him. The silkiness of the wings. The roundness of its edges.

Andrew announces his selection and feels only serene anticipation as the striations of experimentation harden and settle across the bridge of his nose.

When he and Sophie finally exit their respective tents to the anticipating crowd, the gasps drown out the sound of wayward children splashing in the far-off pool.

Andrew blinks, dips his head. He feels their collective gaze searching for scales or some other pointy thing to excuse his choice.

Sophie—a battle-hardened warrior—steps forward, waving to their onlookers with a commanding sweep of her arm. Their eyes move to her, the mosaic of their irises mirroring the path of her hand. Away from him. The crowd parts for her, and Andrew looks on as they slowly re-form in a loose circle, blocking his view while giving her space to march to the snack table. They follow, salivating.

As the party continues in its usual beats—games, pizza, presents—Andrew studies: Sophie’s painted disciples shower her with compliments and take turns resting their hands on her arms as if they could melt into her and become one shared, mighty body.

Andrew tells himself to ignore the whispers of those who relegated him to the edge, where his wings aren’t so pronounced and can better blend with the fence line. He wipes his sweaty palms on his pant legs. They celebrated his change before, he wants to shout to anyone who will listen.

But they’re too busy turning toward Sophie like she’s their sun.

Their child died, their son, their first and only, and only two. Because they could not bear to remember, they refused to be reminded. They packed his clothes into boxes and gave it all away. Toys, books, all the rest, everything: they gave it away. They changed his room into an office, painted it gray, bought black furniture. For months, they worked to remove him from their lives.

But behind the house, under the lilac bush, was a red plastic bucket their son used to fill with dirt and empty and fill again. She saw it when she trimmed the bush. He saw it when he cut the grass. They both saw it, yet never talked about it, never mentioned it, even though each knew the other had seen it, too.

pieces.title: Viking Burial
pieces.author: S. Marie Jones
pieces.html:
My mother’s last birthday gift to me
was a book on Viking burial ships,
the slim volume wrapped in bright paper
just as she taught me—
corners creased
ribbon crossed and tied.

One spring day in Minneapolis,
we had walked together
through the exhibit
on this recent Nordic find.
We marveled at Viking warriors—
their jewel- and fur-covered bodies
resting deep in wooden boats,
forever sailing in soil.

In my mother’s burial vessel
I put the metal measuring tape
she carried in her back pocket,
a box of Starbucks Verona coffee capsules,
a pair of “tie shoes” for getting things done,
and a mystery novel for snowbound afternoons.
I slip in eyeglasses, two pairs,
so as not to leave her eternally
squinting at a blurry afterlife,
and hearing aids,
batteries fresh from Costco.

And how can I forget
the lipstick and silver earrings
she wore whenever she left the house,
even if only for one of
our thirty prescribed visits
to the office of radiation at the Mayo Clinic,
where they aligned their weaponry
to the cross tattooed on her stomach.

The office had a brass bell
to ring on the last day of treatment.
Never admitting the battle was over,
she left the last day, head high.
She refused to ring it.

pieces.html:
We set up our tent at a free campground on the outskirts of Bend. It was late September and we were the only people there, except for these guys. These guys lived in a camper on the back of a pickup truck. They pretended we weren’t there and we pretended they weren’t there. They smashed up picnic tables and built huge campfires. They stood around the fire in hooded sweatshirts pretending they were having a good time, but they weren’t having a good time. Nobody was having a good time.

One night a snow squall swirled down from the mountains, sending these guys—soaking wet and miserable—back into their camper. We climbed into our tent and pulled our sleeping bags over our heads. Later, one guy started screaming at the other guys. It had a tinny sound, coming from the camper, and we could only hear a bit of it. We heard enough, though. It was time to go, I remember thinking, shivering in my bag. That’s it, I thought. Tomorrow, we’ll be moving on.

In the morning the car wouldn’t start. We got towed to a service station. It was three hundred dollars and they had to send for a new alternator. We rented a motel room with a kitchenette and little electric heaters. We were down to our last two hundred bucks, but the smells of soapy hot water and shampoo, and a clean pillowcase, and a hot bowl of soup were something else. We had been living in the car and a tent for months. Then she met somebody, Kathy I think, at a coffee shop. Kathy got her a job, on the spot, as a waitress. I went to a temp agency. I worked for a lady moving furniture, but that’s another story; then I worked at the mill, but that’s another story. Then I got a job digging ditches at a construction site. We told each other that we’d just hole up for a spell, maybe through Christmas, and maybe through the winter. We were getting along then. Things started to settle.

She started hanging out, regularly, with Kathy. They went and had tea together, then they went for walks, then they went for dinner. Kathy brought her into a spiritual something, some kind of group, or circle. She wanted to explain it to me, she told me one night, but I wouldn’t understand. So I went to high school football games. Or I sat in the diner, drinking coffee and watching the passing headlights. Some nights, I stood in the parking lot behind the motel and I stared up at the snowcapped mountains lined up behind it, like outbound planes on a runway. The mountains made me homesick, in a way. But they also kept us detached from the other world, the old world. This was all good, I told myself. This was all going to work out.

The ditch-digging job happened at the edge of a canyon. Ditches had to be dug by hand, with shovels, out of a bank of red clay. They couldn’t bring heavy machinery, on account of the canyon. The company poured cement into the ditches I dug, to make foundations for ski condos. Five weeks, six weeks; clay and roots and rocks and freezing red water; pickaxes and shovels and rebar. The sad man with the beet-red face working next to me, who couldn’t bend his knees, never said a word. My hands were cracked and broken. I could feel my ribs pressing on my wet shirt. Pine tar and dried clay stuck to my pants. Colder winds blew down from the mountain, pressing down on the trees, flooding the canyon.

The foreman had a big rolley moustache and suspenders. He screamed at me sometimes. But because he was born again, he wasn’t able to cuss when he did it. One afternoon I dug through an underground cable, and the power went out in the company work shed. He came out red-faced, hollering. I committed what he said to memory. I was dying to tell her what he said:

“Git your sore bottom up to them site five cables like no bending mother, you big paper place maker baby, and splice up that blue mother-hugging bunny; not that way, this way, you smell-pantsing hippy nose-ringer.”

I recited it all the way home that night; I couldn’t wait to tell her. Nose-ringer? Where did he get nose-ringer? I thought she’d find it funny. It was a three-mile walk from the site to the motel. Now it was early December. There was a foot of snow on the ground, and another round coming over the mountain. I clenched my frozen hands to my chest, my wet pants frozen to my legs, chuckling to myself. I was going to make her laugh. I was going to make her laugh!

I found her sitting at the little kitchen table. Her arms were folded and tears streaked her face. It was like being in the car, in the rain, all over again.

“What happened?”

“The roads are closed.”

“What do you mean the roads are closed?”

“The snow closed the roads over the mountain. Kathy told me. The state troopers closed the roads. She told me sometimes they stay closed until March.”

“But, I don’t know,” I said. “I mean, I’m sure they plough the roads.”

She banged her hands, palm down, on the table. Then she folded her arms again.

“How did you let this happen?”

“How did I let what happen?”

“How did we get stuck here? Why didn’t we keep moving?”

“I don’t know.”

“I think you wanted this to happen.”

She repeated this a few more times, whispering at the end, like she’d been whispering it to herself for days. Then she got up and slammed the bathroom door behind her. The room was so small that the door almost hit me in the face.

pieces.title: Twenty-Seven
pieces.author: Sanya Hundal Bery
pieces.html:
A man on the J train has a rat
on his shoulder. It’s been there
for as long as he can remember.
I tend to it now, he says,
since I realized it’ll never leave.

If I feed my rat
my sadness
will it grow to be the
most interesting thing about me?

The subway man is only Rat Man,
but I can be more than that,
I think.

Delight and I
exist so well together. We

call my mom when rhododendrons
are in bloom, and sit on that rock
by the creek. Watch the sun dance
across the water, those sweet,
blinking jewels! And,

it is because it is.
Which is what my doctor said
when I asked why

my right foot is half a size
larger than the other.

Kiley had told me that rats
have rootless incisors. Meaning
their teeth grow continuously
for their whole lives.

My rat was once all teeth.
Fang forward in an overdone
unbecoming sort of way.

I was so sad I was angry
and now I am so sad
I am trying
to be grateful.

OK, I’ll trim my rat’s teeth.

The Rat Man and I both
get off at Canal St.
A woman pounds her fist
against a dinner plate.

Nothing is to be trusted,
she yells, the Appalachian
Mountains are older than
Saturn’s rings.

I look it up, and it’s true!
It is because it is.

Four hundred million years
apart and yet
both existed before my sadness
and both will exist after.

But I, only with it.

I, only with my sadness and
all seven of Saturn’s rings and
the Appalachian Mountains,
which are also older than
the ozone layer and
every rat, and their unending teeth and
my mom, who calls to say
the lemon tree has sprouted
a green fruit, which is
encouraging. It just needs time,
and Maria, who waits for me
at the corner, because she always
takes off work on my birthday.

pieces.title: Half-Remembered Goodbyes
pieces.author: Elliott Fielding
pieces.nomination_line: “Half-Remembered Goodbyes” is an Inkhorn Review 2026 nominee for The Best American Essays.
pieces.html:
The last time I saw my dad? It must’ve been at the hospital, when I, the only surviving power of attorney, authorized the ventilator to keep his sepsis-ravaged body breathing. I probably managed goodbye and I love you, but I hope he couldn’t hear me and was unaware of the tube pushed down his throat.

The last time I saw my mother, it must’ve been a holiday visit. I’m sure there was a tearful farewell: her tears and my attempts to hide my annoyance. I hope I was successful.

I knew it was the last, the last time I saw my childhood dog—now the recipient of my parents’ doubly empty-nested grief—three-legged, riding in her hand-built cart, bumping along the forest path that would’ve been a respite, before.

The last time I saw my brother? This one I can’t place, not even within a month, although I know we were both adults—me at college, he striving to make his way in business and art—never thinking any visit could be our final one. In the absence of memory, I create. How about we were at his sculpture studio? How about he was showing me his latest piece? I’m sure I said something so smart about its lines or weight or form. He asked me about school. Yes, I think this actually happened. I showed him my tattoo. He scolded me, where my parents had not, something about the sanctity of the body, half teasing, half serious. I can imagine his wry goodbye, a little dismissive, not weighted with meaning. He was never big on goodbyes, and neither am I. But I wish I remembered, all the same.

pieces.title: Metal Storm
pieces.author: William Doreski
pieces.html:
Harsh metals fall from the sky.
We shelter in the oyster bar
and leave metallurgy to others.

We agree that our planet
must have run over a small
but elemental lump of debris.

The oysters are good this month.
Their life spans may be modest,
but their vacant shells honor

the creature that created them
thanks to twists of evolution
no one could have seen coming.

Some of the falling metal
has already oxidized greenish
or reddish or black. When

this peculiar storm ends, people
will scoop up the shards to sell
to tourists and eager scientists.

We’ll remain seated and sipping
Tanqueray gin and tonic.
We’ve already eaten a dozen

mildly protesting oysters.
Their shells pile up on a plate
much as the alien sky-elements

collect in the street, sharp edges
daring us to touch them and risk
wounds too celestial to heal.

pieces.title: Sled Dogs
pieces.author: Michele Catalano
pieces.html:
She’s reading a book of poetry called Drunk Drivers Always Have the Right of Way, settles on one called “Tale of the Yukon”; four lines, one stanza, a poem ending with a man eating his sled dogs.

She’s had too many chocolate martinis at book club, and the words on the page start to blur. She thinks it’s a good poem. She takes the book into the bathroom and sits on the cool tiled floor. She leans her elbow on the toilet lid and waits. She knows she will be sick soon, the question is, how sick. She has passed out from drinking more nights than she hasn’t, awoken only by her cat pawing at her face.

She opens the book again, back to the poem about the sled dogs. She thinks about the words while her stomach turns, while the sour, familiar taste in her throat feels like a threat. She opens the lid, waits. The floor spins and she spins with it and then she is on the floor face-to-face with her quizzical cat and she thinks she just might die there, she might never get up, and her cat will eat her before making its exit and, later, someone would write a four-line, one-stanza poem about her.

pieces.title: I Am Either Hallucinating This Morning or Living It
pieces.author: Sambhu R.
pieces.html:
Either way I cannot tell the difference. A seam opens
along the bathroom tiles, their ripple design, as I pour

bucketfuls of wakefulness over my arched spine.
Salt water comes frothing out, throwing up a swirl

of moray eels & stingrays, the spray bisecting my face
into wet & dry skin as though there is a neat way

of dividing the world into what one can atone for & cannot.
When the walls breathe the scent of blood & ambergris

from a bygone century, I wonder what you would have to say
about these piecemeal extinctions, how they thwart our desire

for a spectacular end, how remorse becomes self-indulgence
without an audience. Today, I am either having trouble

with nouns or with things refusing to comply with their labels.
The mirror is a casket from which my left eye gleams,

the chair a reliquary for your absence. When I hold a glass
of water, my fingerprints outgrow my grasp, the loops

& whorls extending to every dry riverbed where a sangai
or a golden langur might have collapsed on its hind legs,

its mouth parched before the silt. Last night I dreamt
I heard my father’s voice over the phone, all the vowels

incised out of it with shears so that what reached my ears
was the sound of hydrangeas wilting in the acid rain.

As the light slants in through the leaves mobbing the windowsill,
the dust motes refuse their orbits, migrating towards the borders

of my face. The room unbuilds itself, its architecture a faint
vein pulsing under lichen & bark. The roof lifts, all wingbeat

& feral throat. At what point does a body dissolve
into its setting? If I lie face down on the floor, I can feel

my heartbeat thud back from the loam. Undertow
for undertow. If I own my story the way the dead grasp
at the living, I know I will never haunt.

pieces.title: There is safety in birdsong
pieces.author: Sam Agar
pieces.html:
It’s always been easier on the island. Less ground to cover, more room for escape. She arrived shortly before the end of everything. She’s lost track of how long it’s been and when she tries to guess, her mind becomes warped with thoughts of days and months and years, all jumbled into one endless before, bringing up burps of panic and dread. It’s better to focus on what’s in front of her: canned food, bottled water, packets of oats and grains. Two weeks after the collapse, when time was still manageable, she found a small row of shops and a few scattered cottages, all abandoned, all good foraging for what was left behind. They are not infinite, these boxes and bags and bottles lining her walls, and she must face the terrifying thought of after. She would like to start a garden. She wakes up at night thinking about all the things she does not know. There are still books, piled dusty and rotting in the small library at the centre of the island where the bells used to toll. She wanders the shelves searching desperately for all the answers she might need, the ones she hasn’t even thought of yet. There is a section on DIY and gardening and yet the words fall flat. She is used to being shown how to do everything.

When the warnings came, early and often, she did not look up. It was only when the panic began to distract and multiply that she took action. She bought a freshwater pen, designed by a celebrity survivalist. When it did not arrive, she wept over the amount of money it cost, and the realisation that none of that mattered anymore. She has done well to get this far. She has always been good at being alone, it is essential to her survival. No one cries out for her or reaches for her hand and for this she is grateful. She finds a collection of seeds amongst the debris of a garden shed. Tomatoes, potatoes, and carrots. Celery and onions. She starts with a sunflower seed. At first there is nothing, an emptiness which she watches from the corner of her eye as she pretends not to sink hope into the dry soil. And then a shoot of green—small with promise and disappointment. It is her fixation; it is her infant. Each day it grows is a gift. When she has to move it to a bigger pot, she is sick with nerves, cooing and whispering and praying. Once it is almost as tall as her, she knows she should plant it outside but is not ready to lose it yet. She walks the island every day, watching for changes, making mental notes, faced always with her ignorance. There were experts once, people who would know what to look for. Sometimes she screams into the emptiness, swallowed whole by her echoes until her throat is raw and silenced. She paces against the worry that something should be done and that she should be the one to do it. Her sunflower begins to die, wilting and tired. Its loss is brutal, and she grieves.

The robin is the first to come back to her. Tiny and undeniable, it haunts her every step. She is convinced it is an imagined companion. She has long since accepted that she will lose her mind. This is the beginning. It is there again on her next walk, bold and quick, teasing landings ahead of her feet, hopping away before her pace can catch up. It won’t let her get too close, but it eats the grains she scatters with each stride. She watches in awe, breath timid against this new wonder. It has been so long; it is poetry and music. And then it is joined by another, bigger and braver. It is a shock at first, when she first hears them sing, foreign and familiar all at once. Trilling in her ears as she wakes, confusing her momentarily as she reaches for an alarm that doesn’t exist. She gets used to it so quickly, and with it a sense of guilt and anxiety arrives. She must be grateful; she must not take it for granted. There are new birds to look at, small and blue, tiny speckled brown, vibrant orange. Blue tit, wren, bullfinch. She reads the names from a mouldy children’s book, forgetting them almost immediately after turning the page. She carries it around with her, so she can check, so she can remember. It’s like a drug, this reawakening, and she can feel the absence of others more than ever. While before it was useful, now it feels like a suffering, a painful wonder of who and how many.

She finds eggshells on the bank of the river, dropped across her path like a gift. She collects them gently, thinking of the chickens that she will likely never see again. They break against her hands as she buries them in the soil. It is a sacred act. She plants the tomatoes and potatoes and carrots. She plants everything she can find, digging and toiling and begging promise. Please don’t die. Please come back. She does not know how often to turn the soil or what is the best time to sow. She does not know about fertiliser or nutrients. She gives herself blindly to this revolution, hoping she can play a part. She is hungry for it. As the world becomes green around her there are new discoveries to be made. Splashing in the river, rustling in the trees. She is careful with her tread; she is an interloper, and this place does not belong to her. When the harvest arrives, she is pagan in her embrace, dancing and singing with the rising sun. There is too much for just her. She laughs like a child, naked in her joy, running to the centre of the island, where the bells will ring again.

pieces.title: Pine Needles
pieces.author: Jay Caselberg
pieces.html:
A cat approaches
I must clarify quickly
I am not a tree

pieces.title: How Now Brown Cow
pieces.author: James Lewis Huss
pieces.html:
I went to two old high schools in
my Carolina town.
The one was home to white students,
the other home to brown.

The old white school was girded by
the nicest homes around.
The black school had a graveyard by
the playground. And a cow.

pieces.title: In a Stranger’s Kitchen
pieces.author: Nan J Bauer
pieces.nomination_line: “In a Stranger’s Kitchen” is an Inkhorn Review 2026 nominee for The Best American Essays.
pieces.html:
In a sleepy town an hour from our cramped Manhattan apartment, in a stranger’s kitchen, we house-sit one November. Onions and celery sizzle on the stove, sweet potatoes bubble in a pot, a splayed turkey begs me to stuff it with sage and bread.

It’s the second Thanksgiving for me and this second husband. At our first Thanksgiving, I got drunk, because who doesn’t get drunk on Thanksgiving? And I talked about god, my eyes blazing and words slurring, less because I cared all that much about god, more because I cared about my folly in making the decision that this man was the right one to follow the first husband, the dead one, the one I still loved but a thirty-year-old has to move on, doesn’t she?

And on that first Thanksgiving this second husband smirked and rolled his eyes and apologized to our guests on my behalf as he saw them out the door, holding my hair back as I knelt over our toilet, and why wasn’t it even clean?

Away from the city, the pressure of living together in a tiny space, this second husband tops my glass with merlot the color of plasma, an upgrade from the cheap shit I drank before I met him. And then he says something I don’t agree with, and of course I can’t remember it now because he said shit I didn’t agree with all the time. And every answer to every statement stays calm on purpose the louder I get and he walks over, his hands raised to put on my shoulders.

And the next thing I see is the point of the stranger’s paring knife dripping with juice from the blood orange I’ve been slicing aimed at him and he puts his hands in the air and backs away.

And I start laughing at how ridiculous I must look, how ridiculous I am, pointing a knife at this man who tells me he loves me, worships me, the man to whom I answer, I love you too (but never I worship you, too because, no matter how much wine I drink, I cannot lie) and I can tell by his eyes round with disgust that he is not in on the joke.

I hear him mutter psycho through the side of his mouth when his back is turned and I am still smiling, because I am not a psycho, just a bad actress in a terrible play.

I set the knife down. Hang my head as I shake it. Apologize with a rueful laugh sorry. Turn my back on him, recommence slicing the orange with the stranger’s knife calm like him.

In the quiet, the yams bubble. I hear his socked feet walk up behind me. I feel him put his arms around me, brace his chest against the flinch of my back and I wash down the shame that sticks in my throat with what’s left in my glass and say sorry I don’t know what that was about I’ll never do that again as his chin grinds into my shoulder in the rhythm of his nod.

I silently inventory my better weapons. I can slash and burn and do not leave marks.

Your glass is empty. He pours more wine, for himself then for me. In the stranger’s crystal glasses.

In this strange, sorrowful kitchen that smells so good, as if it is overfull with love.

pieces.title: Father’s Day
pieces.author: Don J. Kraemer
pieces.html:
The only call I got, mid-brunch—
reframing the eggs, the bacon:
outdoors glancing bees perusing
the benches: an inescapable sun
and voices silenced but one.
Imagine this filmed: the father pleased
his son
(they always ask,
“Your only son?”)
remembered to call, then
ablated by the small,
total, dejection on the
line, as if the inner
voice of avenging angels, vows
of terror to come.
The call drops. “Who was that?” the
gathering asks. My ungathered self
shrugs—my son arrested again,
facing serious time.

Those disturbingly disciplined straightforward
Dobermans in Philadelphia, the pair of them
shot out of darkness, cornering me, refusing
my ruses. Waited for the owner to show, make
things better. No one showed. It was nearly
the New Year. Who’d be on the street in this
cold, car broken down, walking the two miles
home in a T-shirt, fair game for unleashed
dogs doing their duty. Don’t believe in bail,
in innocence, in mercy, in adult compromise—
my cries for help unheeded. Thank god for
public transportation: a city bus boomed by.
The dogs turned their mythic heads that way
and I ran, crossing the boulevard and jumping
onto a parked car. The dogs followed a few
yards into the road, surely breaking their
training, which after a few barks—desultory,
to be sure—reeled them back into darkness.

How often I swerve into the light of that long-
ago scare. Because it holds me I can’t change.
What it did to me a mosquito could do worse.
Not a reminder of our fragility, then, but maybe
of how to read? A streetlamp would have helped.
Those dogs were as beautiful as my son, as
purposeful as a fix. Imagine the dogs he
encountered all those nights on the street, the
smell of them, the sounds that literalized any-
thing mythic. It was still reading. Did you exist
there, in the dogs you did not adopt, who licked
your blood, or is existence here only, outside my
fear-wracked reckoning?

As scared as ever—me, long-
dead dogs, the curb we
stepped off, my first
White Russian
after, elegiac
phones, un-
lickable
pain.

pieces.title: The Incredible Shrinking Coffee Shop of Paris
pieces.author: Elizabeth F.A. Meaney
pieces.bio: Elizabeth F.A. Meaney is a dual citizen of the United States and Ireland living in Paris. She has an MFA from Hunter College and has published three novels.
pieces.bio_html: Elizabeth F.A. Meaney is a dual citizen of the United States and Ireland living in Paris. She has an MFA from Hunter College and has published three novels.
pieces.html:
It really was a hidden gem—so hidden, in fact, that Hannah walked past the coffee shop three times before she realized it was there. And the moment she stepped inside, she regretted it.

Birch was in one of the little picturesque side streets lost between the Rue de Rivoli and Opera, perfectly located for Hannah to visit before her 4:30 ticket time at the Museum of Decorative Arts. It was un coffee shop even in French, which meant that, unlike un café, it had more matcha and bubble tea than actual coffee, except the agonizingly slow Vietnam drip coffee that the barista would explain to you as you nodded knowingly, really clueless.

When Hannah finally spotted birch, whispered in pale script on a pale wood panel above a doorway, she pushed the door open. She walked up the narrow aisle between the stone walls lined with wooden benches, instinctively sucking in her breath, feeling like a bride or a criminal at a courthouse. All the eyes of the people packed along the benches were on her as she brushed against their coat sleeves and stepped over their backpacks.

This gallery-style seating area had no chairs, not even the rattly bistro ones from a café, and no stools either, not even the ratty carpeted ones from a pub. But then the end of the aisle opened into a wide and bizarrely modern counter area that looked like a UFO, with six baristas in white caps bustling inside a glowing neon circle.

One paused scooping boba balls to toss Hannah the menu, and Hannah, who’d been expecting a QR code, was surprised to find six laminated pages flapping from a metal ring so large she could have worn it as a bracelet. Coffee, iced coffee, tea, iced tea, milk tea, fruit tea, boba, infusions, add-ons, syrups . . . She turned the pages around the big ring helplessly until she realized she’d been through the menu twice, then called out an order at random, the top choice on the page she was on. A tattooed barista fiercely whisking matcha nodded, and a girl with big gold hexagonal glasses tapped her card and handed her a heavy buzzer almost the size of a Frisbee, with red lights circling around it.

There was a narrow slice of bench on the right side of the shop, and Hannah squeezed herself into it. A young guy in an oversized hoodie made room for her, and she crossed her legs tightly under the skinny tin table in front of the bench. When she set the buzzer down, the table nearly tipped under its weight, so Hannah stared in amazement at the girl to her left who had managed to balance her phone, her laptop, and a large boba tea with tapioca balls like eyeballs on the same-sized table, and who was typing calmly within the zen calm of her Lo-Fi Girl headphones. How did she do it?

Hannah was American. That had to be the problem. But she wasn’t that American! She had never craved howling prairies and tumbleweeds, never admired the Grand Canyon or yawning deserts of Utah. She had worn skinny jeans, slept in a single bed, never needed bumper alleys in a bowling alley. She was an East Coast girl, from a town whose only landmark was a historical property called “the Skinny House,” and she had been happy there, and even happier in the cramped coach seat of the sleek jet that had propelled her to an even tinier and tighter-packed continent.

Now she felt overstuffed and suffocated. Struggling out of her coat, she elbowed both the hoodie boy and the laptop girl, who gave a calm smile and continued typing. Hannah rolled her coat into a ball on her lap, balanced her purse on top of her coat and the buzzer, still red, on top of her purse. Like the toppling tower of teacups from Alice in Wonderland. Two remarkably tall hikers with overstuffed backpacks strolled into the coffee shop and headed to the counter to browse the plasticky menu. A Great Dane leading a girl with a high ponytail came in next, and they joined the couple at the counter to peruse the matcha options.

She wasn’t comfortable anywhere here! It was time for Hannah to admit it. She had struggled with skinny shop aisles and spiral staircases, elevators like rattling coffins, rented clown cars and studio apartments cramped with dollhouse furniture. How romantic it had once seemed to her when the couple in L’Auberge Espagnole kissed on the narrowest street in Paris with the man’s sneakers tipping off the curb edge. Now she had no desire to bump noses with anyone in that cobblestone alley.

She wanted to breathe. The longer she sat with the buzzer’s red lights circling her tightly crossed knees with her legs going numb, her elbows clamped to her sides, the more she craved it. Oh, how she wanted the prairie, great sweeping wheat fields she had never known, wide and wild enough for a tornado . . .

The buzzer roared to life, lights flashing green. It slid off her purse and clunked to the floor, and the purse and coat followed it. Her tower was toppled. The buzzer growled angrily against the metal pole of the table, drowning out the quiet conversations around her, and she dropped to the floor with her cheeks hot to grab it. When she looked up, she saw that the laptop girl had bent down to help her, and was holding out her purse.

“Are you okay?” the girl asked in English, tugging her headphones down to her neck.

“Oh—yeah—thanks.” Hannah grabbed the purse and coat and stuffed them on the bench, then promptly bashed her head on the metal table when she tried to stand up.

Straightening the table, she hurried back to the counter to dispose of the violent buzzer and find out what in the world she had ordered. It was alien purple, topped with a cloud of foam, in a heavy ceramic mug like half a volleyball. She stared at it so long that the barista in the gold glasses frowned.

“Vous avez bien pris le ube, non?”

Ube. Yes. Definitely.

Hannah placed one palm under the flimsy rectangular tray and cupped her palm around the mug, which had no handle, balancing it carefully as she made her way back to her slot. Her hips bumped on both sides this time—people must have pushed their tin tables out—and she found herself stepping over chunky sneakers as well as those big hiking packs, and the panting Great Dane stretched out at a metal water bowl. She was so relieved to reach her own table safely that she set the heavy mug down too hard and a purple wave sloshed over the side, flooding the tray. Much more gingerly, she picked up her coat and purse and backed herself into her slot on the bench. Then, after rolling the coat and restacking her lap pile again, she managed to take her first tentative sip.

“C’est bon, l’ube, non?” The hoodie boy turned to smile at her.

“Oui, très bon,” she lied, and faked a smile.

She was OLD. That was an even more depressing realization than being American. Look at these kids! In their chunky white grandpa sneakers and baggy sweater vests, when she at their age had worn low-slung Brazilian jeans to look like Christina Aguilera. Everything they wore now was three sizes too big, including the hoodies and headphones—and when had Parisians started wearing puffy coats? Hannah had been so sure the wool pea coat rolled in her lap would be the right thing for Europe, but now she was surrounded by overstuffed black down jackets, and, what’s more, the people were comfortable in them.

Hannah was less comfortable than ever. The next time she lifted the heavy mug, she was forced to keep her elbows pinned tightly to her sides. Her friendly neighbors on the bench must have scooted closer to make room for all the newcomers streaming through the narrow doorway. Come in! The more, the merrier!

She still couldn’t say if she liked the ube or not, or how it was supposed to taste, or if she should have gotten rice milk instead—if she should say it “wasn’t too sweet,” which seemed to be a compliment these days. Weren’t lattes supposed to be sweet? And weren’t cafes supposed to be comfortable? How else had those Viennese philosophers lounged and smoked and plotted their revolutions? Hannah was not in a position to plan or lounge, not with the stones of the wall digging into her spine and the bench under her so narrow now that she tipped forward, her tailbone just balanced on the sharp edge.

But others were chatting. The laptop girl was still typing, maybe writing a Gen Z masterpiece about love in an elevator, and someone across the aisle was so relaxed they’d stretched their legs all the way across the aisle, which was otherwise completely occupied by the Great Dane, bookended by the two hiking packs. Hannah couldn’t do it. She was old, she was American—she could admit both now—and she could never belong here. She belonged in a wide leather booth at a midwestern Denny’s. She belonged back in her grandfather’s ancient Plymouth, rattling to the beach with the windows open and rolling in the back seat without a seat belt. She wanted—needed—to sprawl, and saw so clearly now that she always had: the strain of tiptoes to stretch herself taller, all the snow angels and cartwheels, a whole year in third grade learning the splits, spreading, pulling, reaching—

Her elbow, reaching without her meaning to, knocked the metal table. The flimsy tray slid, the heavy mug tipped the table, and she grabbed with both hands to right it, but too late. The table clattered to the floor, the mug cracked in half, and an ocean of foaming ube flooded the coffee shop. The Great Dane yelped and leaped to her long legs as Hannah flung herself down, her palms in the spreading purple lake. Her coat and purse had tumbled into it, too, but she couldn’t worry about those, not when she had to stop the flood, not when she was scooping too-hot latte into her cupped palms with nowhere to put it.

Ruined! Her panicked thoughts raced. The coffee shop floor would be ruined, and its reputation, too. This place used to be a hidden gem—she could already see the online reviews—and now it’s just American tourists. MIDDLE-AGED American tourists.

Her tiny square napkin flashed white surrender, soaked, and sank. Her tray was sailing away. The purple foam was surging towards the backpacks, towards the chunky sneakers which were all bright spotless white, and she was helpless to stop it.

Then she turned and saw help. The laptop girl was kneeling beside her, with Hannah’s wool coat draped over her legs. She had saved it from the spill and was pressing a larger napkin to the stain as tenderly as if it were a wound, soaking the purple away and reassuring her:

“I think it will wash out.”

Hannah turned the other way to see the boy in the hoodie carefully picking the cracked porcelain shards of the mug out of the purple foam.

“Be careful,” he said in French. “Don’t cut yourself.”

And others were helping—everyone was helping, the young hipsters squatting in the spill, careless of their white sneakers, the hikers pulling rags and towels from their packs to sop up the latte.

“Now she’ll finally have to toss that smelly old T-shirt,” the hiking guy joked with Hannah in French. “Thank you for that!”

The Great Dane, over the shock of the spill, was now licking happily at the edges of the foam, and Hannah, blinking in bewilderment, offered up her cupped hands to be licked, too.

Even the floating UFO of the counter hovered closer now, glowing right above her, and the benevolent aliens had brought high-tech help. The hexagon glasses girl started hoovering up the spill, while the Great Dane barked in indignation and tried to lick it up first. All the young people were laughing. The laptop girl had her warm shoulder pressed to Hannah’s, so close Hannah could hear the music in her tugged-down headphones, and it was an old song she knew.

“Would you like another drink?” Gold Glasses asked Hannah when she had finished vacuuming. “Maybe a regular latte?”

Hannah nodded. A foaming surge rose inside her—happiness, belonging—and her heart was a heavy, brimming cup. The floor was shining, cleaner than before, and all of them were still squatting around the shining spot like it was a campfire.

And the stone walls curved to hug them all closer.

after James Wright, “Goodbye to the Poetry of Calcium”

I do not even have salt to rub in my wounds.
My mother would have given them willingly,
but I could not decide between a fragment
of her hand or the shoulder of her robe,
and so she remained stationary, intact.
My father’s request, I ignored
but I could not claim her body, destroy
the picture she made overlooking human
life, the cities we had left,
cities of longing and mundane humanity.

Oh father! It seems such a power—your lot
to forget—a daydream of quiet and promise.
Mother—still—waiting for rains in the desert
to wash her back into the wadi,
spice for some man’s food,
begin again as his tears,
her salt falling to an underground
stream working its way back to the sea.

pieces.html:
My sister’s truck took the sharp turns of the mountain road with ease until, near the summit of Mount Wilson, she herself did not.

Mum selects the Flowers4Ever Heavenly Sunset Funerary Trio.

At 7:40 p.m., someone called 911 about a driver seen falling from a truck as it sped around a curve. The person disappeared over the cliff and the driverless vehicle crashed into a ditch along the mountainside.

I text Dan, Angela’s last guy, a picture and description of Mum’s selection from the florist’s website.

The Heavenly Sunset Funerary Trio is a colorful reflection of an exuberant life.

The truck wasn’t my sister’s. It was Dan’s and had, according to the police report, been stolen that afternoon.

The week before, the truck had been keyed. Gouges found on the hood looked sorta like an F and a D and a U. There was a misshapen heart on the driver’s door.

Heaven. Mum believes Angela is there now and is beautiful again. We saw her bloody and bandaged, wired and tubed. Her swollen face slowly turned white.

Exuberant. Yeah, Angela definitely could be. When she was, she’d dance on the fire escape and on street corners, and people would call her the Thursday-Friday-Saturday Night Party Girl.

This sympathy rainbow of love and remembrance

“There’s a rainbow over the spot,” Mum declares, wiping her eyes.

I nod. I open Google Maps and follow hairpin curves along California State Route 88B, wondering which one is the spot.

includes a casket spray, a standing spray, and a vase tribute arrangement. $680.

Ping: Dan will contribute $150.

“That’s not much,” Mum rumbles, “considering he lived with her and must’ve loved her.”

I don’t nod.

Mum notices. “You don’t think he did?”

“No idea,” I reply. “We know nothing about him.” His number was in Angela’s phone under Fucker. “We haven’t even spoken to him yet.”

Says Mum, “You’ve never lived with a man.”

Unclear, according to the police, if the driver’s door opened unexpectedly or if Angela opened it, if she fell out of the truck, or jumped.

Sunflowers, gerberas, snapdragons, roses, and carnations in rich orange, loving red, and hopeful yellow.

I’m to take home the tribute vase arrangement after the service, to add a pinch of sugar to every water change and cut off the ends of the flowers daily. I’m told I don’t always take good care. “You were the big sister.”

Enhance The Heavenly Sunset Trio Funerary Display with thoughtful wellness gifts like comforting herbal teas, a cuddly teddy bear, relaxing scented candles,

Mum had hoped that Angela would turn her life around at You Are Well House. Mum had borrowed against her condo to pay for six weeks of inpatient care there, and sold her Subaru for four more. Sobriety was my sister’s mountain.

or a keepsake photo frame.

Mum is a no to all the other pricey funeral add-ons, but yes to this. She wants a dozen frames in pearl with etched doves.

Since I’ve failed my sister, I’m to gather happy photos—“Angela must be sober and smiling”—and to ask “that man” for what he might have of my sister so long as they’re not of her partying.

A satinette ribbon adds a finishing touch. Available in sky blue, navy, forest green, yellow, pink, or black.

This is nice. A black ribbon woven through the flowers would be striking and poignant. “It’d really set off the oranges and reds.”

Mum stares. “Black? Really? Is that what you think of your sister?”

No. But, well, kinda. Sometimes.

I finish my cold tea, stand up, push the chair under the table. I try to kiss Mum’s wet cheek, but she pulls away.

Oh, okay. All right. “Be back in the morning to pick photos for your frames,” I snap, then stomp down the hall. Hearing her sob back in the kitchen, I quietly shut the front door.

Personalize the ribbon with a farewell in gold or silver. Choose from:

May you rest in peace.

With deepest condolences.

We miss you.

Thank you for your love.

Or create your very own sentiment.

I do. Following a black ribbon of highway on the dark drive home, I think of many:

We should’ve talked. I could’ve called. Didn’t even know you had moved to California.

Tell me about Dan. The when, the how!

Was it an accident? I need to know, tbh.

Didn’t really believe Mum when she said she paid for rehab with a lottery win, did you?

Hoping you like the flowers, my little Angie Banjee.

pieces.html:
It is a ghost posed on my lips.
—Jorie Graham

You find yourself back at the station,
at the centre of four escalators.
Ahead, the clocks click
against their dental frames
and rehearse their mudras.
You are expected at Shanghai, so you
buy a ticket for nowhere,
between Suzhou and Hangzhou, to
a place you cannot pronounce.
At the gantry, you stand between Manual
and Automated, willowy like a toilet brush.
The workers see your red passport, wave
you through. You thought the mountains
would be blurred like memory;
instead, you remember constant velocity.
The osmanthus trees are swaying still.
You hated China, complained
to your mother. Everywhere back home:
落后. You wished the entire nation
would undulate and fall like a leaf
but the muhly grass in the park that day
was pink and maneing themselves in the wind.
And it’s clear: mother had forgotten
her Shanghai dialect. She was great
at it, once. Now, she is someone from China
touring gardened condos in Singapore
and performing it as a party trick.
Language, erased. Religion, effaced.
Which idols did they worship,
what currency did they offer
besides their vase-fluted bodies?
Chairman Mao, may you live for ten
thousand years, mother and father
kept chanting in their sleep.
Darkened bodies fall past the platforms
and into the slipstream.
Moving to an emptier compartment,
the waitress says behind her red flask
you need to buy tea to sit.
Relief sweeps across her face.
The steel wheels of escape shriek
across your mind. You lean back—
Zhu Bajie’s rake scrapes your shoulder.
High-beam headlights ignite
the karsts by a lake,
engrave the ninth slickenline.

The train slows for the tunnel.
Tea leaves sink.
The glass slowly fogs.
Yet, the split-flap sky manages to perfect
its lapidary hues lengthwise.

pieces.title: That one time in December
pieces.author: Sanya Hundal Bery
pieces.html:
we drove up to Lake Michigan. The
ice sat crisscrossed on the sand.
It was so rare, that
earnest stage of becoming.
The waves too, partially glaciated,
but the wake still fluid enough to
offer itself to the shore. The whole
spectacle, impossible to hold
in my salty, East Coast mind. And
still, there it was. I said,
I think I’ll write about this, I
just don’t have all of it yet. You
didn’t need to ask have what. Simply
reached behind my ears, to gather me
in your hands. Then, off you went,
barreling towards the water, mouth
open. And,

you know when you search for
that fallen thing under the couch
and there’s that one moment
right before
where its edges lightly brush
against your outstretched fingers?

Yes, it was just like that.

pieces.html:
I’m writing to inform you of your father’s death. I hope you’re sitting down for this. He was mauled by a Komodo dragon after jumping the fence at the Omaha Zoo. The missing chunk was substantial. A watermelon’s worth, maybe more. Witnesses at the scene have all said he didn’t plead for his life with the enormous lizard. You should be proud of that. A lesser man would have begged. Not that it would have made a difference. The dragon is an inveterate killer. Besides, everyone knows that Komodo dragons don’t speak English. They speak Indonesian.

I apologize for my attempt at humor. Something about seeing the aftermath of a Komodo dragon attack has a way of decentering a person. There was an awful lot of blood. Did your dad have some sort of medical issue? The inside of the enclosure looked like the stage at a Gallagher show. Prop comedian. Before your time. More than one witness claimed that for the briefest of moments, your father had the dragon in a headlock. It looked like he might “put it to sleep.” For the briefest of moments. You should be proud of that. It takes enormous courage to jump the fence at the Komodo dragon exhibit at the Omaha Zoo. What’s more, it takes enormous physical strength to put a Komodo dragon in a headlock, even if for the briefest of moments. You’ll have a story to tell when your father is absent on Career Day at your elementary school. The other children will surely think you are so “cool.” That’s something you can be proud of.

The bite pressure of a Komodo dragon is incredible. I’m not a scientist, but I’d say it’s roughly the equivalent of at least three or four alligators. At least. That should give you an idea of just how impossible it was for your father’s thigh to resist amputation. You shouldn’t be ashamed of that. No one’s thigh could stand up to that kind of scrutiny. I was told on the scene afterwards by a particularly morbid zookeeper that a Komodo dragon could easily bite through solid steel. Incredible, I know. But he’s the expert. That’s a factoid you can share with your classmates. Trust me: they’ll find it very impressive. First you tell them that, then about the headlock, and lastly you mention the absence of pleading. The way to do it is like it’s no big deal. They’ll think your dad was a real stand-up guy.

It’s important for you to understand that recently your father had been under a lot of pressure at the office. His creative work for “Diet Doctor Zippo” was not doing so well. This is what your mother told me. It was, to use her words, “bombing spectacularly.” Hence, perhaps, his decision to jump the fence of the Komodo dragon enclosure at the Omaha Zoo. Was a lot on the line with Diet Doctor Zippo? More than you will ever know. That’s something you should be proud of. Your dad ran with the “big dogs” and never cracked up. Well. Almost never. And can you really call it a crack-up if, for the briefest of moments, he was the one who had the dragon in a headlock?

I think not.

You might be wondering why I’m writing you this letter. I’ve been asking myself that question. The easiest explanation would be because your mother asked me to. But that doesn’t feel quite right. As one of only two public safety journalists at the Omaha World-Herald, I feel a kind of professional obligation to the story, and I think it would be remiss of me to leave any loose ends. That includes your future grief. Right now, I’m certain, your mom is telling you a story about how your dad is at the North Pole with Santa wrapping presents. Textbook. If it’s any consolation, that’s what my mom said when my dad never came home from Iraq. And yet I hope this letter comforts you upon discovery of the facts. If you’re anything like me, it might engender in you a lifelong compulsion towards truth. If I may offer you a little bit of advance advice on that front: it’s okay to lie, sometimes, and especially if your marriage is on the line. Your first love is the only real one. Everything after that is an act of imagination. But that’s a digression. I’m sorry. My thoughts have been scattered since reviewing photographs of the incident with your father.

Twenty years from now, when you’re graduating from college, there’s no telling what the world will be like. I doubt journalism as a professional activity will exist. You’ll likely wake up early, eat a bowl of fungal protein mush, and rush to your job as a warehouse associate shipping off-label automatic cat feeders to childless project managers on the West Coast. Don’t be sad. No one gets what they want out of life. Not exactly. Not all the way. Only in snatches, the briefest of moments. That split second your dad had the dragon in a headlock, for instance. A moment like that can make a life. It can make the whole miserable ride worth it. I hope one day you find your dragon and “put it to sleep.” If I’m being honest with you, I hope I do, too.

Until that day, I wish you all the best.
